speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) to an announcement of ' Le Canada ' to-day. It reads as follows :

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The Intercolonial Railway will have this year a first-class service.
From the 1st of July next, two luxurious trains will leave Montreal every day, except Saturday, for Sydney and Halifax.
The maritime express, which under present arrangements, leaves at noon, will steam out at eight o'clock in the morning. As for the additional train, the Ocean Limited, it will leave at eight o'clock in the evening and reach its destination within twenty-four hours. The latter service will, no doubt, be very well received by the travelling public. The trip will be shorter, as the night train does not stop at all stations. Besides, passengers will for the first time view in broad day-light the magnificent scenery of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
Numerous visitors are expected this year. However, it is possible that the St. Louis exhibition and the presidential election may divert from the maritime provinces a goodly

proportloin of the tourists who visited them last year.
By this announcement we are told that there will be every day two express trains leaving Montreal, one in the morning and one in the evening, except on Saturday. I would like to know the reason why, if two trains are to leave Montreal on the Intercolonial Railway every day, we are not to have a service in our district on Saturday.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The announcement in ' Le Canada ' is in part true in respect to the proposal to put on an additional train between Montreal and Halifax. The trains going east have always left on Sunday both by the Canadian Pacific Railway and by the government road. It has not been suggested that there should be any change, and if an additional train is put on it would probably leave on the evening of every day excepting Saturday. That would be the present intention. My attention has not been called to any question as to that arrangement.
Why not on Saturday ?

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and with the permission of the House, may I be allowed to remark that it is a great inconvenience and drawback to our district that people travelling from Montreal eastward should not have a train on Saturday. Business men and others going down to the seaside desire to go on Saturday. This is a great drawback to the people of the district of Quebec and I do not know any reason why we should not have a Saturday train. Trains leave the maritime provinces for the province of Quebec on Saturday, arriving on Sunday, and I do not see why trains should not leave the province of Quebec on Saturday for the maritime provinces, arriving on Sunday as well.

speakerposition: topic
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I would like to inquire from the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) as to what progress he has made with the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Railway Companies about making such connections at Brockville as will allow the mails to be carried through from the west on the day train. I brought this matter to his attention two or three weeks ago, but I have not had any report from him yet.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) did call my attention to it and I stated then as I state now that it is not a matter under the control of the Department 105	I

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: of Railways and Canals, that we have established a railway commission with large powers in connection with the railways of the country. The Department of Railways and Canals has control of the Intercolonial Railway, or of the government system, but it has not control of the other railways of the country. The question raised by my hon. friend is one which should be determined. I think, if at all, by anybody, by the railway commission. As I then stated to my hon. friend the attention of the commission was called to the matter. What it has done I am not in a position to state, but I presume that it is taking action in connection with the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to say that I
do not understand that the Railway Commission has anything to do in connection with the carrying of the mails. The government makes arrangements with railways for carrying the mails. We pay the Grand Trunk for bringing tjie mail from Toronto and it is supposed to be delivered to the Canadian Pacific Railway. The mails arrive at Brockville a little after three and they do not arrive in Ottawa until seven the next morning, whereas they should be here by five o'clock the same evening. I do not know whether it is the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals or the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Muloek) who is responsible, but somebody should see to it that the mail service is improved.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Department of Railways and Canals has nothing whatever to do with mail contracts either with railways or in any other direction.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon the Postmaster General (Sir William Muloek) at least, ought to see to this. Last year there was no difficulty. The mail train left Toronto early enough to make connection at Brockville and the mails came through. This year a change has been made by which the fast train passes the mail train at Kingstqn with the result that the mail train does not make connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway train for Ottawa at Brockville. This is a great incon-veaience to every person east of Toronto, because we cannot get our mails here by way of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think it is worth the while of the hon. the Postmaster General to see that an arrangement is made, so that we can get our mails the same day as that upon which they are despatched. If proper connections were made, I could easily get letters written at noon at my own home at five o'clock the same day. Now I have to wait until the following morning. I think this is a great inconvenience and one which we should not have to submit to.

My hon. friend from South i.eeds (Mr. Taylor) brought this subject up
EDITION	..

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
some time ago and I made inquiry then.
I tound that the mails were despatched by the Grand Trunk express which reaches Brockyille at the hour named, and if it is on time they are transferred to the Canadian Pacific at Brockyille and brought to Ottawa. If the mails fail to reach Ottawa the same day it is not because of their not being on the Grand Trunk train, but it is because of the train not making connection.
The Brockyille train coming to Ottawa leaves Brockyille before the mail train on the Grand Trunk reaches Brockyille.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: No, it does not.
Yes, it does.

I come here nearly every Monday, and I think I ought to know. The fast train passes the mail train at Kingston. We get that train to Brockyille and if we do not get there in time to make connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, we have to go on to Coteau..

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: The mails for Ottawa that come from Toronto are transferred at Kingston junction to the fast Grand Trunk train due to arrive at Brockyille before the Canadian Pacific Railway is due to leave Brockville.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think the hon. the Postmaster General is wrong except in regard to the Toronto mails. The mails gathered up at the different stations east of Toronto continue on the mail train until it arrives in Brockville. The fast train only makes three or four stops east of Toronto and passes the mail train at Kingston. If the mail train were permitted to run right through to Brockville it could get there in time to make connection. The train is held at Kingston to allow the fast train to pass, and the latter train does not take on any of tne way-station mail. I come down every Monday and I know that the passengers make connection, but the mails do not. If a mail bag from Toronto comes by the Grand Trunk Railway, it may be handed over, but there is no general mail delivery by the mail train at Brockville. I am sorry the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) is not here just now for I am quite sure he would endorse this complaint. We are paying large sums to the railways for carrying the mails, and we might as well be living in the country as in the capital, where we can only get our mails [DOT]every twenty-four hours.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext:
We offer the mails to every train that will carry them, and if this train does not stop after leaving Kingston until it gets to Brockville, I would like to know what can be done by us. The Grand Trunk Railway regulates its own time table ; it is running a fast express train between Toronto and Montreal which only stops at nine stations going west and four-Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
teen stations going east, although there are fifty-five stations on that line. The mails from the west by the morning train are transferred at Kingston to the fast tram that is due to reach Brockville before the Canadian Pacific train leaves there. Inasmuch as the fast train does not stop between Kingston and Brockville, I suppose the mail cannot be put off at intermediate stations. There have been frequent interruptions in the mail service at Brockville, because the Grand Trunk has been several times late, and the Canadian Pacific Railway has felt it its duty to start on time in order to make its own connections. I inquired from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, if they V: ould hold their train at Brockville, but they have replied that though they are anxious to oblige the public, they have to make their own connections at Smith's Falls and Ottawa.
I may say that I have received information which may or may not be correct, that passengers have frequently seen the Canadian Pacific Railway train steaming out of Brockville just as the Grand Trunk Railway train was arriving, and that in many instances passengers from the west have been subjected tp great annoyance because of this.

The difficulty would appear to be, as the Postmaster General intimates, that the Canadian Pacific Railway train is not held sufficiently long at Brockville. This train sometimes stops fifteen or twentv minutes, or even a half an hour at Smith's Falls, but it will not postpone its time of starting from Brockville.

I call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that we have only one mail a day on the Ottawa and New York Railway between Ottawa and Cornwall. I can assure the hon. gentleman that this is a grpat inconvenience to the people of Cornwall and to the people living at the different stations along the line. I would suggest -to him that he should arrange that there should be a mail sent from Ottawa to Cornwall by the morning train as well as by the evening train, and that from Cornwall to Ottawa the two trains daily should be utilized for the carrying of the mail. If you mail a letter in Ottawa at six o'clock this evening, it will not reach Cornwall until about seven o'clock to-morrow night, and it is usually not delivered until the following morning. I have discussed this matter with the people of Russell, Finch, Chrysler, and other towns along the line, and they all agree that it would be a great convenience if the two daily trains on the Ottawa and New York Railway carried the mail. I ask the Postmaster General to give this matter his immediate consideration.

I cannot see how the Postmaster General -can excuse the Grand Trunk Railway for the poor accommodation they are giving us east of Toronto. I have no feeling against the Grand Trunk or any other railway, but I suppose the

country pays for carrying the mails, and if so we should have a service adequate to our requirements. I can tell the Postmaster General, that for a great number of years the mail train from Toronto made connections at Brockville, and it can do so still if it starts from Toronto a few minutes earlier. There is great inconvenience caused to the people in my section of the country, at Brighton, Colborne and Grafton and other places because of the present arrangement. The very fact that the mail train remains over at Kingston to allow the express train to pass, accounts for the tardy delivery of the mail in Ottawa. If I understood the Postmaster General properly, he said that he could not control the carrying of the mails. Well, that is a sad plight for a Postmaster General to be in. If through him the country pays the railways for carrying the mails, surely he can insist that the country gets a proper mail service.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I see the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Harty) now in his seat, and I think he will corroborate what I state. 'I think the hon. Postmaster General is in error in saying that the fast train carries the mail. He has led us to believe that the fast train does not stop at Gananoque. It does stop there, but it takes on no mail. The mail train gets to Kingston a good many minutes before the fast train ; but it is held there for thirty minutes for dinner, whereas if it went on it could reach Brockville and deliver the mail to the Canadian Pacific Railway train ten or twelve minutes before its time of leaving. If the statement of the hon. Postmaster General were correct, that the mail was transferred to the fast train at Kingston, the people west of Kingston could have their mail carried to Ottawa ; but there is no mail clerk on the fast train and no transfer. If the hon. Postmaster General is paying the Grand Trunk for carrying that mail, he should insist that instead of staying at Kingston it should go on to Brockville, where it would arrive in plenty of time to deliver the mail.

I will read a statement from the controller of the railway mail service :
Mails from Toronto and the west, and also mails received by the postal car clerks between Toronto and Kingston are transferred at Kingston Junction from the postal car train which leaves Toronto at 8 a.m. to the fast train which leaves Toronto at 9 a.m., to connect at Brockville with the Canadian Pacific Railway train leaving Brockville at 2.45 p.m.
Such connection has been missed seven times during the past month, which is no doubt due to the inclement weather, and the high water at different places along the Grand Trunk Railway between Toronto and Brockville.
The fast Grand Trunk Railway trains, operated between Montreal and Toronto, only stop at nine stations going west, and fourteen 1054
stations going east, and there are fifty-five stations between Montreal and Toronto.
The controller might add that there is seemingly no inclination on the part of either of the railway companies above mentioned to make connections at Brockville in cases when the trains of either railways are a few minutes late, and connections should be made, by trains of either railway systems awaiting five or ten minutes at Brockville.
I think it depends on the goodwill of the railways. If they were desirous of making connection at Brockville, they could make it in most eases.

speechtext: House in Committee on Bill (No. 72) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
May I ask my hon. and learned friend the Minister of Justice if he has come to any decision as to the amendment which I proposed to the committee last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have had an opportunity to consider the amendment suggested by my hon. friend last night, and the conclusion we have come to is that we must amend the General Railway Act so as to make applicable to all railways in this country the provision which my hon. friend desired to insert in the Grand Trunk Pacific Act.

I do not think we can accept that suggestion at all. The railway now7 under the consideration of the committee is in altogether a different position from the railways in general in the country. It is called the National Transcontinental Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Pacific.

It was introduced into this House as the National Transcontinental Railway and the principal object of the government is stated to he to continue the Canadian or British policy of carrying the traffic from the west to our own eastern sea-board. If this policy is controlled by a board of directors the majority of

whom are not British subjects, we cannot believe that it will be carried into effect. But there is not the same reason for such a provision in the case of some railways that run from one province to another or through a part of the Dominion. In some instances it would cause great inconveniences to have the general railway law amended in the direction mentioned by my hon. friend. The question does not come up in the same way, and the same reasons do not exist. Why should it have been necessary to include in the Canadian Pacific Railway Bill the proviso that a majority of the directors shall be British subjects if it is not necessary to do the same thing in the Bill now under consideration ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have only this observation to make in answer to the remarks of my hon. friend from Montmorency, that the government is of opinion that at this stage of the development of national railways in Canada, they should he operated by boards on which British subjects are in the majority.

Then there can be no objection to amending this law to that effect. I would call the right hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that this question came up last year, when in answer to my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), he promised that the contract would be amended to that effect. But the discussion went on from day to day, and the contract was not amended. So that we find to-day that the promise my right hon. friend made was not implemented. I am sure it was not any fault of his ; it escaped his attention. But if it was so important last year that my right hon. friend promised the House that it would be done, it is equally important this year ; and in case it might escape the right hon. gentleman's attention before an amendment is proposed to the General Railway Act, I intend to press this amendment.

In view of what the right hon. gentleman promised last session, 1 think it is impossible for the government not to accept this amendment. If this Bill goes through and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is built, we shall only have in this country two great railways-the Canadian Pacific, of which it is provided that the majority of the directors shall- be British subjects, and this railway. I want to draw the attention of the House to what the right hon. gentleman said last jear. On page 8066 of ' Hansard,' I moved :
That Bill (No. 64) he not now read the third time, but that it he referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of amending section eight by adding thereto the following words : ' The majority of the directors of whom the president shall be one shall be British subjects.'

The Prime Minister then said :
If my hon. friend will accept a suggestion I would say that while I think his amendment is a good one and I do not see any objection to it, I think we had better introduce it into the Bill confirming the contract which will come later. I am prepared to accept this amendment, but I think it would be better to put it into the Bill confirming the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
I understand the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to say that this provision will be made a part of the contract ?

Yes.
There are no two meanings to that language, and I do not think that the right hon. gentleman can successfully evade the question by saying there should be a general law governing it. We only have two great railway companies, and I would like to know if the Grand Trunk Railway have put their veto on this proposition. Has there been any intimation from the Grand Trunk Railway that the government must not consent to this thing, and that the directorate should not be compelled to be composed of a majority of British subjects ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is assuming that the right hon. the First Minister is objecting to this provision as respects this company, but I do not see that he has any grounds for his contention. What the Minister of Justice has said is that the government were prepared to adopt the principle as respects this and other companies as well. My hon. friend says that there are only two great railway companies in the Dominion ; but even if the others are not so great, conditions might arise [DOT]which would lead our neighbours on the other side of the line to desire to obtain control. If it be a wise proposal that the directorate of one company should contain a majority of British citizens, the proposition is equally wise with respect to other companies. It is difficult to see why it should be wise in the case of a line 3,000 miles long and not wise in the case of another line only 2,000 miles long. I fail to see any harm that will come if such a provision be applied to the smallest railways of the country as well as to the largest.
How is it possible to make a general law governing the question ? How would you apply it to the Michigan Central, which runs between Michigan and Niagara Falls ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That company operates under the charter of the Canada Southern, and there would be no difficulty in having a majority of British subjects on the directorate of that road. Of course, if there is any existing board of directors, on which there is at this moment not a majority of British subjects, I would not advise in favour of turning these men, who are not British subjects, out of office, but I take it

for granted that a reasonable provision will be made and reasonable time allowed for the reorganization of such a board. If the proposition be applied to all railway companies, I cannot see what possible harm can result.
That is all right so far as it goes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It could not go any further, could it ?

Take the position of affairs which existed last year. We were then promised that this amendment would be added to the Bill and that a majority of the directorate would have to be British subjects. This year we have another promise. We are promised that a provision to this effect is to be added to the General Railway Act this session, but the leader of the House may go to the Yukon, and we do not know when he will return. The Minister of Railways may continue to be absent from the House, so that we will have nobody to look after the amendment. [DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman himself may not be here.
I will be here to stay. If it is the intention of the government to put this in a general Bill, there can be no objection to putting it in this special Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to lack faith in the opposition. Even if some of the members of the cabinet should be absent, hon. gentlemen opposite will be here, and it will be their fault if the matter is not brought up.
We cannot always do what we want.

I understand the Minister of Finance to give as a reason why this amendment should not be adopted that it is the intention of the government tc consider whether they shall introduce into the General Railway Act a provision to the same effect, which shall apply to all companies. That may or may not be a thing that will come to pass within the next few years, but whatever may be the position of the government with regard to companies generally, there are special reasons why such a clause should be inserted in the Act relating to this particular company. There are reasons why this provision should apply to this company, which perhaps do not exist with regard to any other company. This is called a National Transcontinental Railway, and if there is any company in existence which should have its board composed as this amendment proposes, it is this one. I think, whatever faith we may have in the Minister of Finance, we may have some hesitation in believing that it is likely he will carry out his good intention. I do not doubt for a moment his good
faith, but would ask him to consider this. Suppose he comes next year with a Bill to introduce this amendment into the General Railway Act, making it apply to all railway companies, where is he going to be with regard to the Grand Trunk Railway ? He will find a great many difficulties about applying his proposed amendment do that company. Almost every shareholder and bondholder interested in the Grand Trunk Railway is a resident of England or of one of the British islands. Those people have acquired for the last half century their interest in that company, knowing they had a board in England, knowing that the board met there, and that they could attend the half-yearly meeting of that board and discuss there their interests and criticise the conduct of every president and director. I think there might be a very strong case made out against the proposition of the government to make this clause applicable to every company. Certainly there would be very strong ground shown. I think, in opposition to making such a clause apply to the Grand Trunk Railway. If that be so, if there be one company to whom such an amendment might possibly be an injustice, is it not clear that we should now lose the opportunity of making this amendment apply to the one company to which we know it ought to apply ? And what is the company to which it ought to apply ? That is the point of the amendment and we cannot understand why hon. gentlemen should refuse. What possible objection can they have to providing that the board of directors who are to control this Natioual Transcontinental Railway shall be British subjects ? Are they going to leave it open to foreigners, aliens, to manage the policy of the Transcontinental Railway, the national railway of Canada ? That is the effect of the opposition to this amendment. Though it might be prudent and wise to make that clause apply to half the railway companies of Canada for one reason or another, there cannot be one sensible reason given for objecting to it with regard to this particular railway. And it is now. when we have an opportunity of applying it to this company that the government hesitates, and says no. I would like to know their reason for it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) says that there :s no objection to it but he intends to do something else. That is no answer-no answer whatever. This company when it is floated should be floated on a distinct understanding as to the character of the board that is to rule it. The company should not be allowed to go upon the market, create their holdings, elect their directors, and then, we afterwards come and say to them :	You must change all that ; ' we
did not put it into the Bill when we had the opportunity to do so ; we left you free to take what course you pleased ; but nowr you must dismiss these alien directors.

I say this is the time when it ought to be clone. There may be in the future, many reasons why the Minister of Finance cannot carry out his proposition even though be would like to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) says he cannot see any good reason why the majority of the board of the Grand Trunk Pacific should not be British subjects. In that statement we agree ; We know no reason why the majority should not be British subjects. But we see no reason why that should not apply to every state-aided railway in Canada.* And, if the hon. gentleman sees any objection to that, I would like to hear him state it. We can see no objection.
Why not adopt the amendment ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Wre say we will do it. But we say we cannot see any reason why the hon. gentlemen opposite should single out this particular railway for such an amendment. We mean to have it made applicable to all state-aided railways in Canada.

The reason is that this is the one railway incorporated in this country which, the Prime Minister and his followers tell us, is to be the National Transcontinental Railway. That railway has special obligations to this country ; it has enormous powers in the country ; it has powers on the very point that we have been discussing as to diverting our traffic from Canada; and for these reasons we do not want aliens controlling this company of all companies.

It seems to me that the experience of the last year would indicate that it would be well to deal with this matter now. Last year a similar amendment was offered by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), but, on the assurance of the Prime Minister that that provision would be incorporated in the Act, that amendment was withdrawn. That was a year ago; and still, although the Prime Minister asserted then, and asserts now, that he regards it as a matter of importance, in fact of necessity, that such a provision should be made, we find that a member of this House is again offering the same amendment, which proves satisfactorily enough. I should think, that the provision lias not been made. Now, it is quite possible that what has been neglected for a year may be neglected for two years ; and, unless some good reason can be shown why this provision should not be put in this Bill, it seems to me a case has been made out sufficiently strong to justify us in making this amendment to the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The matter is simply this. A proposition was made last year by the hon. member for East Mr. BARKER.
Toronto (Mr. Kemp) and I acceded to it, and told him that I would make it a part ot the Transcontinental Railway Act. l am sorry to say it escaped my memory. Apparently, it escaped the memory of hon. gentlemen opposite also, for we were not reminded of it. We are reminded of it now, and we say we intend to apply this principle not only to this particular railway, but to every state-aided railway corporation.
When ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This session. If we fail to do it, my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) will remind me of it.

It does not seem to me exactly proper that this should be applied to every railway corporation, because there are some of them that, although built on Canadian soil, have been built largely with American capital, their principal owners reside in the United States and their earnings must go mainly to (hat country. It is only reasonable that the parties who raised the bulk of the capital should have some control (over the enterprise. Hut, if we make provision in the Railway Act compelling every railway company operating any portion of its line in Canada to have a majority of British subjects in its directorate, it would be unjust to many of these concerns. Take, for instance, the railway passing through the south-western part of Ontario, the old Canadian Southern, now the Michigan Central, it would be hardship to provide that a majority of the directors of that road should be British subjects. The old Grand Trunk itself, has nearly as much of its line in the United States as in Canada. But for the fact that the bulk of the capital put into it, outside of the assistance given by this government and the provincial governments, was raised in England it would be a hardship, perhaps, to insist upon such a provision in that case. There are cases where the bulk of the capital for the construction of a railway was raised in the United States, and the earnings should go to the people in that country. In such cases it would hardly be fair to compel them to have a majority of British subjects upon their directorate. But this Grand Trunk Pacific road is different from the others. From the very inception of it, the great claim made by the Prime Minister was that this was going to be a road not only Canadian, but every foot of it on Canadian soil, carrying traffic to build up Canadian ports and absolutely free from foreigh control. It was to be owned and controlled by Canadians or British subjects, and was to be the great defence of Canada should the United States do away with the bonding arrangement. In every wTay it was to be Canadian. For that reason, the Prime Minister says, we are justified in giving it very large assist-

since ami great consideration. But, as we have been assured that the object of giving that assistance was to make a road eminently and entirely Canadian, we ask that the necessary proviso be inserted in the Bill that the majority of the directors shall be British subjects so that we may be guaranteed against the danger of foreign control of what we are told is to be the great National Transcontinental Railway. And yet the Minister of Justice says that is not a proper thing to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh. no.

No. The contention of the government is that it is not a proper tiling to put such a provision in this Act. We claim that it is, and the objection to the contention of the Minister of Justice that this should be in the General Railway Act and should apply to all railways is that it could not be properly done, and it would be an injustice in many cases to foreigners who own and control roads in Canada to-day. If it were inserted in this clause it would be distinct and applicable to one road at least whereas it could not be applicable to all roads. I am told there is such a provision in the Canadian Pacific Railway Act, then why should there not be one placed in this Act ? It was not left to the Ceneral Railway Act in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but was placed in a special provision in the private Act. The Canadian Pacific Railway, although it was a company in the interest of Canada, has some of its line in the United States, through the state of Maine and in the west. This road the First Minister claims, is wholly Canadian, and why should he object to adding a clause in the Bill by which the majority of the directors who control this road and Who would be responsible for its operation should be British ?

There is a great deal in the contention of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). Reference has been made to other lines in Canada, built to a large extent by American capital. The Canada Southern has been mentioned. Every one who knows the facts in connection with that railway knows that the local traffic from the section of southern Ontario through which it runs wTould not support that railway at all. and that the railway would not have been built, if it had not been able to depend for its existence on the through traffic from the western states to the eastern states. It would not be fair to place that road on a par with the National Transcontinental Railway. I cannot see why. if the government say it should apply to all railways, they should refuse to put it in this Bill now7. That is beyond my comprehension. because it certainly ought to apply to this road. Little or no American freight is to pass over this road which is purely a Canadian national road, and if it
does not apply to this road, why should it apply to any in the country ? It is built by the money of Canada and I presume this is the proper Bill in which to place an amendment of that character.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen are surely borrow'ing trouble. When we come to introduce amendments to the General Railway Act we shall take care that all interests will be properly safeguarded. In the meantime it must be borne in mind that our desire is that this railway should be constructed, owned, operated and controlled absolutely by British subjects.
Has the Grand Trunk Pacific any particular objection to a clause of that kind being placed in the Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether they have or not, nor do I care.
As this is a government owned by the Grand Trunk Railway, I thought it might be worth while consulting them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not at all ; this is a question of public interest.
Amendment (Mr. Casgrain) negatived.

built and I think it is not too much to say that some of these branch lines will probably carry a larger proportion of the western traffic than will the extreme eastern section of this line. As a result, in all probability, the main line trade may be taken from the western section to our eastern ports and the various eastern points not by a continuous run along the eastern section, but by running along part of the eastern section to some one or more of the many branch lines that will be built. It also goes almost without saying that some of the branch lines that in all probability will be built will not be successful lines, and will be lines over which there will not be any of this main traffic. Under para-giaph 11 of the agreement, those lines oo which there has been no such traffic or along which no special business has been created will have to be taken over by the government at a price as agreed on. I am not discussing that or any questions of liability under that paragraph ; but I want to deal with the other lines for which no provision is made under this contract. As the Grand Trunk Pacific has, under -this agreement, haulage rights and very clear haulage rights after the fifty years have expired, and as they will have had their organization and their western connection, all of which is arranged for by this Act, this contract and the one passed last year, I think we can take it for granted that after fifty years have expired the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific, or whatever it may be at the end of that time, will have certain branch lines the operation of which is absolutely necessary to the successful running of the eastern section by the government. I submit this amendment largely on that account. It will be very essential for the government to have other connections than those which have proved a failure under Grand Trunk Pacific operation. The only branch lines for which provision is made for their taking possession of under the contract are those which have proved a failure to those who have operated the line during that fifty years or which are a failure at the end of fifty years. If this contract is left as it is and if it is clearly understood that the government have no right to take over the successful branch lines, the branch lines which are absolutely necessary to the successful operation of the eastern section, it will mean that the government will be so handicapped at' the end of the fifty years or that they can be so handicapped by the Grand Trunk Railway 'Company if they perfect their organization as they undoubtedly will that the government will almost be compelled to make a renewal of the lease under section 24, I think it is. of the original Act. Unless the government contemplate building parallel branch lines and making connections to points to which these successful branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific have carried Mr. IA VEIL.
trade. I therefore would submit that this amendment is a reasonable one and that it is not inconsistent with this contract ; nor can it in any sense of the word be said that its adoption would prevent the whole contract being carried out. I do not, for myself, admit the argument but it apparently has been used as an argument by the lion. Minister of Justice and other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, that any amendment which materially interferes with the contract cannot be accepted. I submit that this is an amendment which does not materially interfere with the contract. It simply gives the right to the government to take possession of the lines which are absolutely necessary to the successful operation of the eastern section, and I would ask the government to take it into their serious consideration and to see if such a section could not be incorporated in the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The object the government had (in view in connection with the project was ' to secure an outlet for the trade of the Northwest by the shortest, most commodious and most direct route to the summer ports on the St. Lawrence and to the winter ports in the maritime provinces. Then, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company chose to ask for permission to build branch lines from this main line from Winnipeg to Moncton, one of which would extend to Port Arthur, or to some other port on Lake Superior, another to North Bay and the third to Montreal. If at the expiration of the fifty year period the company chose to continue in control of their branch lines then to operate them successfully it will be necessary for them to use the main line of the government road and to that extent the government will benefit by the successful operation of the branch lines. Can it be imagined that these branch lines cannot be successfully operated ? The one to Port Arthur will enable them to communicate with water navigation at the head of Lake Superior, the second will enable them to communicate with their Ontario system and the other to Montreal places them in touch with an ocean port at the head of navigation. These branch lines must necessarily be operated by the company and operated successfully and in proportion as they operate these branch lines successfully the government, if the main line reverts to the government, will get the benefit of that operation. As far as the other branch lines are concerned my hon. friend (Mr. Lavell) has to remember that there is no present power in the company to build any branch lines beyond the three which I have mentioned. Their power to build branch lines is limited to the three which I have referred to. If in future it is their desire to build other branch lines which may not be operated successfully it will be for parlia-

inent when it gives permission to build branch lines to attach such conditions to the permission as will enable parliament to deal with the question before the lease ends. At the present time the lease is applicable only to three lines which I have mentioned.
Mr. LAVE LI,. Could they not get authority to build branch lines from Quebec or Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is another question.

I think that the indications are strongly in favour of the proposition that they can get that authority. I submit that no branch lines should come under this section unless the authority of parliament has been obtained. I admit that my amendment does not touch that. But. I had it in my mind that the company were able to get authority to build branch lines. It has been suggested that the line being built by the province of Ontario may be transferred to the Grand Trunk Pacific and if so it will be transferred simply under its Ontario charter. Again, there may be branch lines built in the province of Quebec to reach Montreal and in other directions. It is a little difficult to say what lines may be built fifty years from now, but, dealing with the point which the hon. Minister of Justice has affirmed, if these lines can be successfully operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company why should they not be more successfully operated by the owners of the eastern section ? We found in the discussion that took place when the orders of the day were called to-day, that it is not always the easiest thing in the world to make satisfactory connections between lines whose business interests may be separated for the time being and it may be possible that these branch lines which the Grand Trunk Pacific may get permission to build may be used for the purpose of bull dozing the government into giving them better terms. I think the whole argument comes down to this that if these lines are successful it is in the interest of the government to operate them in connection with the eastern section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there seems to be a theory in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite that some of these branch lines which are unprofitable will be left on the hands of the government, that we would have a complaint to make if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had the profitable lines while we had the unprofitable lines ourselves. 1 do not think it is conceivable that fifty years hence any branch line in connection with tiiis enterprise can be regarded as unprofitable. I think that even a moderate anticipation of the growth and progress of Canada for half a century might lead us to hope that any branch line built in connection with
this enterprise will have a fair chance of doing a successful business fifty years from this date. But, I would like to point out that it is quite possible that a branch line might be unprofitable to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and profitable to the government as owners of the main line. What I mean by that is that if a branch line is of short length it would not pay to operate it as an independent road, but it might pay to operate it in connection with the main line which the government would then hold.
Would that apply to all the branches ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might or it might not apply to certain branches, but the point suggested was that the Grand Trunk Pacific would leave the government in possession of the unprofitable branches. I would like the committee to take a more hopeful view of the conditions fifty years hence. It is hardly conceivable that any branch of the road could be unprofitable then.
Then why put the clause in at all ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because, it takes two parties to make a contract, and in an endeavour to make a contract it must be a matter of give and take. This was one of the matters in which the Grand Trunk people thought they saw a concession which they might reasonably ask for. It reminds me of the story of the collier who, when he came before the magistrate and was asked why he allowed his wife to lick him, re plied : * It pleases her and it don't hurt I.' This is a matter that pleases the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and which, as far as I can see, does not impose any risk or liability on the government. But the particular point that I want to direct the attention of the committee to is that it is quite conceivable that a branch line managed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as an isolated and independent line might be unprofitable while it might be quite profitable as a branch belonging to the government who would be the owners of the main line.

I am -willing to be as hopeful as the Minister of Finance, and I trust that at the end of fifty years everything will be as he prophesies. But if so, why does not the government retain the right to buy* such branch lines as we can fairly assume to be the most profitable, and thus have a much more complete railway system under their control. To my mind it is very probable that at the end of fifty years, we will not be exporting a very great deal of our western grain from Canada. I am willing to believe that at the end of fifty years we will have as large a home market for our grain
s the British market affords us to-day.

If that should be the case then a great part of the western produce will be distributed amongst eastern consumers. I think it not only possible but even probable, that if everything progresses in Canada as we hope, many of these branch lines will in the end be carrying grain to eastern consumers, instead of carrying it to the seaports for export. If the government had power under this Bill to take over these branch lines, it would mean that they would have a much more complete railway system. I do not desire to make it compulsory or to add anything to the liability of the country, but the government certainly should have the power to acquire these branch lines if ever it should be desirable to do so.

This lease is for so long a period that it is practically equivalent to ownership of the government road by the Grand Trunk Pacific. At the end of fifty years it will have certain branch lines in operation, and we are giving the Grand Trunk Pacific the right to compel the government to take over at a fair price certain of these branch lines'. Surely it is a matter of. importance that the government should have such branch lines as are necessary in the interests of properly operating the main line. Surely the government should have the right to acquire whatever branch lines are necessary to the working of that transcontinental railway on payment of a fair consideration. That is what the amendment provides. You give the right now to the Grand Trunk Pacific to sell certain branch lines at the expiry of the lease, but you do not retain the right in the government to buy such lines as they may require for the successful operation of the road. That is a very shortsighted policy. If the Grand Trunk Pacific should have the right to dispose of certain branch lines they don't want, surely the government should have the right to buy certain lines which they require for the successful operation of the road.

The Minister of Finance has told us that we do not know what will take place fifty years from now, and he is correct in that, but nevertheless we can tell what took place thirty-five years ago. We can remember that the Drummond County Company which was a lumbering company, built a railway, and after they took the timber off the land they were threatened with bankruptcy, only they were lucky enough to find the government ready to buy their railway. Many of these branch lines to the Transcontinental railway will be built expressly to carry lumber, and we know that when you cut the trees once they do not grow again. Pfty years hence the timber country of to-day will be barren land, and the question will present itself, as to whether there will be a government so good as this one to buy these lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not so good as this government.
Mi-. FITZPATRICK. You will never find the like of this government again.
The country'will never be fooled again.
What happened before may happen again, and it is well that we should take precautions to safeguard the interests of the country.

I fail to see where, in this agreement, the Minister of Justice can find one word which confines the provision to the purchasing of branch lines constructed under the authority of this parliament. The words are as broad as words can be.
In case, during the currency of the lease of the eastern division, the company shall have constructed a branch line or lines.
It does not confine it to lines constructed under the authority of the parliament of Canada ; the company can construct branch lines under other competent authority, and the government can be compelled to buy them. The Minister of Finance says that it is evidently doing something that will please the Grand Trunk and not hurt the government. That is a most extraordinary way of putting it. Let us suppose that there are four branch lines ; the Grand Trunk simply have to say to the government : You must buy branches, one two, and three, but the fourth is a paying line and we will keep it. That is what the hon. gentleman says is doing something that will please the Grand Trunk and does not hurt the country. The amendment simply is. that if the Grand Trunk should say that the government must buy one or more of these branches, the government shall retain the right to buy any other branches they may deem necessary. I cannot imagine two individuals making such a bargain as this where one would not claim a corresponding right granted to the other. This whole legislation is based on the principle that the Grand Trunk is entitled to everything and that the country is entitled to nothing. It is most surprising to me that the opposition to this amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) should come from the government who ought be most anxious to protect the rights of the people.
The hon. gentleman seems to think it matters not. He says : Oh, at the end of fifty years these will all be useful; the traffic will have grown up, and it will be a useful thing for the Grand Trunk to carry the traffic to and from the government road. But that may not be quite in the interest of the government. It may at that time be in the interest of the Grand Trunk to retain a particular branch so as to command the traffic, and coerce the government into giving its traffic to the Grand Trunk. Take the North Bay branch. The Grand Trunk runs from North Bay ; but there are other lines running from North

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Bay also. At the end of fifty years tlie government might want to get that North Bay branch, to carry its traffic down to North Bay, where it would have the opportunity of giving that traffic to two roads. If the Grand Trunk Company retained that branch, it would have the sole connection with the government railway, and it could say : You cannot give the traffic to any one but us, unless you choose to build a branch paralleling our branch. If at the end of the fifty years the Grand Trunk Company proposed to sell all the branches but that North Bay branch, or perhaps the branch to Thunder Bay on Lake Superior, the government could say : These are the branches we want, because if we own the branch to North Bay, we will there connect with other railways as well as yours, and if we own the branch to Lake Superior, we will connect with the shipping. If this clause had been worded as the hon. member for Leeds proposes it shall now be amended, the government would be able to meet the Grand Trunk Company on these conditions; and when they proposed to sell the government some branches it did not want, it could turn around and say to them : If you want us to buy some branches that we do not want, we must have the branches that we do want. But the hon. gentlemen are afraid to accept anything for their own benefit lest it will hurt the Grand Trunk.

It is very extraordinary to find the government giving to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company the absolute right of saying what branch lines they must take. In other words, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, the lines that may prove of no value, on which there may be an actual loss at the end of each year, they are at liberty at any time to unload on the government. Surely the goverment must realize that no business man would ever make an agreement of that kind. It is all one-sided. I am quite satisfied that no minister would make such a one-sided agreement in his own personal business. There is no question that when this railway is completed, there will be some branch lines on which the actual receipts will not pay. If the Grand Trunk Pacific can unload those lines on the government, it is to their advantage to do so. Why should the government not be in a position to take over other branch lines, so that by operating both they could balance matters and avoid actual loss to the country V This is only one of the clauses which the Grand Trunk people have been able to get inserted in this one-sided agreement ; and the government have had to submit in order to please the Grand Trunk. Surely the government should not hesitate to have this clause amended in the way proposed by the hon. member for Leeds. I have not heard any explanation yet from any minister of the Crown why they are
willing to increase the expenditure of the country by taking over lines that will not pay. Before the Bill finally passes, I hope the government will see their way to accept this amendment, because if the government has the right to take over the lines that will pay, the Grand Trunk Company will not be so ready to palm oft' upon them those that will not pay.
Amendment (Mr. Lavell) negatived.

I do not rise at this moment for the purpose of proposing any amendment to the Bill now being considered by the committee ; but I rise to call the attention of the House to a question that is becoming more and more serious as we go on ; and if you decide, Mr. Chairman, that I am not in order in the remarks I make, I will move that the committee now arise and report progress. The resolutions in connection with the National Transcontinental Railway were introduced into this House on the 5th of April last by the right hon. the premier ; they were supported in a speech by the hon. Minister of the Interior; and they have been before the House continuously since that time. Time and again, after speeches made on this side of the House, hon. gentlemen on the other side have thought it incumbent upon them to rise and answer the arguments which have been presented to the committee by those who sit on the right of the Speaker. But, Sir, we have not heard one solitary) word from the Minister of Railways. He has not thought fit to give his opinion as to the merits of the Bill or the resolutions. It is true, he signed the contract between the parties, but since the question has been before the House he has given no sign of life. In fact, every time this Bill comes before the House, the hon. -gentleman sees fit to leave the chamber. I am sorry he is not here today, and I hope that word will be sent to him in order that he may be present, because, although this is not a personal attack, I do not care to attack him, even in his official capacity, in his absence. The defence of this measure has been left almost entirely to my hon. and learned friend the Minister of Justice. I am not complaining that he has not done everything in his power to explain the merits of the Bill and reply to the arguments from this side, and I quite understand that in a matter of this kind the various amendments should be given the benefit of what light his highly trained legal mind can cast upon them. Now and again the First Minister and the Minister of Finance have interjected remarks, but the whole onus of the defence has fallen upon the shoulders of my hon. and learned friend. But apart from the legal points involved, apart from the effect of the different clauses of the agreement, from the legal point of view, there is also to be considered a ques-

tion which affects most materially the Department of Railways and Canals, and that is the general railway policy of this government as set forth in this contract. If there is a man in this House who should naturally be the exponent of that policy and its defender, it is the Minister of Railways and Canals. The government may say that they are entitled to conduct the business of the House as they deem tit and put up any minister they like to answer members on this side. That may be admitted to a certain degree, but there are limits to their discretion in that respect, and these limits are prescribed by constitutional usage and the circumstances of each case. The cabinet is divided into a number of heads, and this division cannot be set aside at the whim or caprice of the government, but is founded upon principle. I have taken the trouble to look at some of the authorities upon this question, which I consider a most important one affecting the constitutional responsibility of the government towards this House and the country. Speaking of the growth and progress of British constitutional methods, Lord Macaulay, in his History of England, says :
It (the ministry) is nominated by the Crown, but it consists exclusively of statesmen whose opinions on the pressing questions of the time agree, in the main, with the opinions of the majority of the House of Commons. Among the members of this committee are distributed the great departments of the administration. Each minister conducts the ordinary business of his own office without reference to his colleagues.
On the same subject, John Stuart Mills, in his ' Considerations of Representative Government,' says :
As a general rule, every executive function, whether superior or subordinate, should be the appointed duty of some given individual. It should be apparent to all the world, who did everything, and through whose default anything was left undone. Responsibility is null where nobody knows who is responsible. Nor, even when real, can it be divided without being weakened. To maintain it at its highest, there must be one person who receives the whole praise of what Is well done, the whole blame of what is ill.
lu Todd's ' Parliamentary Government ' I find the following rule laid down :
One prominent feature in the reforms recently effected in the public departments of Great Britain is deserving of special mention. It is the general substitution of concentrated responsibility in the hands of a minister of the Crown, for the indefinable and irresponsible authority of boards. Formerly it was the custom, in most of the public offices, to place the supreme controlling power in the hands of a board, consisting of several members, nominally of equal rank, and who in their collective capacity met together, at stated times, to transact the business of the department. The Treasury, the Admiralty, the Board of Trade and Plantations, the Board of Control for the government of India, the Ordnance, and the Board of Works, were all originally constituted Mr. CASGRAI.V	"	[DOT]
upon this principle. Gradually, however, it became the practice for the president, or other presiding officer, to transact the ordinary business of these departments, convoking the assistance of his colleagues only upon rare and unusual occasions. But while, in most cases, the outward semblance of a board is still preserved, enlarged experience in the practical working of government has led modern statesmen, with singular unanimity, to concur in condemning boards as instruments of executive authority, on account of their being impediments to prompt action, and destructive of personal responsibility, without offering any equivalent advantage.
Accordingly, with the' solitary exception of the admiralty, all the boards above enumerated have practically ceased to exist. The Treasury Board never assembles, except for certain formal or extraordinary business, its duties being transacted by the chancellor of the exchequer, aided by his colleagues and assistants at the Treasury. The business of the Board of Trade is performed by the president and secretary. The Board of Ordnance has been abolished, and its powers transferred to the department in charge of the new secretary for war. The Board of Control has also ceased to exist, upon the appointment of a secretary of state for India. The secretary for India is, it is true, assisted by a permanent council or board, composed of men who have local knowledge of Indian affairs, and who are possessed of certain specially defined powers ; but the secretary himself has supreme authority, and is personally responsible for everything connected with the government of India.
Thesq citations show that, according to the ruling principles of the British constitution, there must be for every department of state a head responsible to the sovereign, the House of Commons and the people. The same principles and rules have existed in this country for a number of years. It is so true that such a state of things exists in England that, although there should be probably only one Secretary of State, there are five ; and in this instance, as the authorities say, sometimes in urgent cases one Secretary of State can act for another. Todd, in his * Parliamentary Government in England,' says :
So far as regards the secretariat, an interchange of offices is easily managed. In a constitutional point of view, there is but one secretary of state and though the office now consists of five distinct and separate branches, the functions of either secretary, may, upon emergency, be discharged by another.
The same authority, in his book on ' Parliamentary Government in the British Colonies,' says :
It is usual to assign to each of these responsible ministers the charge of a separate department of the state, so as to place the entire public service under the superintendence and control of responsible administrative heads, who possess the confidence of the representative assembly.
As I have said, it was not in vain that this division of authority and control between the different departments of state was made.
*

It was made with an object. In the quotations I have just given, there are three predominant ideas. The statesmen who constitute the cabinet must agree in the main on the pressing questions of the day, but there should be, apart from the general responsibility of the cabinet as a whole, the distinct and individual responsibility ol each member of the cabinet. Not only should the cabinet as a whole enjoy the confidence of the House, but each individual minister should share in that confidence. What this House and country have the right to know is whether upon this important policy the members of the cabinet are in unison. Last year, when this question was first submitted to the House, we had the announcement made that the then Minister of Bail-ways, Mr. Blair, had resigned from the cabinet because he could not agree in the policy determined on by his colleagues. It appears, however, that he was asked to continue in his seat in the cabinet as a silent member and allow one of his colleagues to move the resolution and the Bill in the House. Mr. Blair very properly said : I cannot do so; il' I am not in unison with my colleagues, if I do not agree with them, especially upon an important question of this kind, my obligation and my only duty is to resign from the cabinet. Sir, is it'possible that what happened last year is repeated this year, with less credit to the occupant of the position of the Minister of Railways and Canals ? It is true, the hon. gentleman signed the contract with his whole name, Henry Robert Emmerson. But did he sign it for the price of a seat in the cabinet, for the prestige and influence that goes with it, or even the salary that pertains to the position ? Is it the fact that, although he has signed the contract for the consideration I have mentioned, he has consented to sit dumb in the House-or, rather, not sit at all. but leave the House evqry time the matter comes up for discussion-in order that he may be able to go before his constituents, or before the people of New Brunswick or before the people of St. John where he met defeat a short time ago, and say :	It is true that the government,
of which I am a member, puts this policy before the country, but I am not personally responsible for it, and you will look in vain in the pages of ' Hansard ' to find a single line to show that I stood up in the House to defend that policy. I do not know whether that is the position, but it seems to me we have a right to hear from the hon. gentleman's own lips whether he agrees with his colleagues^ in putting this policy forward, and saddling the country with the enormous expense which must result from it. Of course, the cabinet as a whole is responsible, and every member ef it is responsible to the House and the country for this measure ; but I say that the country are entitled to give the praise or fix the blame for this policy more particularly on the individual
whose department it most conceims. Let us look at the past history of this country. What happened when the Canadian Pacific Railway resolutions were brought down in the session of 1880-81 ? If hon. gentlemen will refer to the first volume of that session, they will find that the resolutions were introduced on the 14th of December, 1880, by Sir Charles Tapper, who was then Minister of Public Works, having in his department the railways and canals, because a separate department of Railways and Canals had not then been established. Suppose that Sir John Macdonald, then Prime Minister, said to Sir Charles Tapper :	This is
a Bill which pertains to the department over which you preside, but I am going to place it before the House myself ; suppose that the Minister of Justice of that day had said that he was going to put these resolutions before the House ; knowing Sir Charles Tupper as I know him, I am sure he would have said : you have no confidence in my ability and you fear that I cannot move these resolutions or defend them, and I think he would have found in that a sufficient reason to leave the government of the day. Not only did he move the resolutions, but he took upon himself the weight of the debate. This 'Hansard' is full of speeches made by him at that time. He it was who bore the brunt of the battle, he it was who got all the abuse from his opponents, when they said that the Canadian Pacific Railway was an enterprise which was going to bankrupt the country. And to-day it is he who reaps the credit, I may say the glory, of having carried through this House a measure which has done so much to build up our country and make it great. When the Yukon Railway resolutions were introduced, it was not the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice or the Minister of the Interior who introduced them. The government then had a strong man at the head of the department of Railways and Canals, hon. Mr. Blair, and he it was who introduced the resolutions in this House. And when the extension of the Intercolonial was proposed, again Mr. Blair took charge of the Bill and piloted it through the House. This is the first time such a measure as this has come before the House without being fathered and conducted through all its several stages by the minister to whose department the question properly appertained. Let me put this question :	Supposing an
important measure appertaining to the department of the hon. the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) had to be put through the House, does anybody suspect for a moment that that hon. gentleman would take a back seat and allow his colleagues the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Finance to introduce and conduct it through ? Suppose that some question of importance relating to the Department of Justice was to be put before the House, does anybody think for an instant that my hon. and learned

friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick), would allow anybody else to take charge of it-

Because I think my hon. friend has too much self-respect to allow anybody else to take charge of a Bill relating to a matter in his own department. I can understand that, when this policy was to be inaugurated, being a great policy in the estimation of hon. gentlemen opposite, there was some excuse for the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) introducing it in the House seeing that he was practically without a Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Blair who was then at the head of the Pepartment of Railways and Canals, could not approve of it. But now that he has a Minister of Railways and Canals, and now that the policy has been inaugurated and it is simply a question of a measure to amend the contract, I' say it is strange that it should be in the hands of any member of the cabinet except the Minister of Railways and Canals. It appears strange not only to gentlemen on this side of the House, but also to hon. gentlemen opposite that, when this measure comes up, the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) not only has nothing to say, but walks out of the House, as it were, snaps his lingers, treating this House with scant courtesy and certainly not with the respect which is due to it. I say that the Minister of Railways and Canals by his conduct has lost, to a great extent, the confidence of the House and of the country. Why is it that he is not here to defend this scheme ? If he does not disagree with his colleagues on this subject, I am afraid he will make the House believe, make those who sit around him believe, certainly w-ill make this side of the House and the country believe, that he is not able to defend this measure before the House, that he has not sufficient ability to do it. I would regret hon. gentlemen coming to that conclusion, but it is a conclusion which must of necessity impose itself on the minds of hon. members of this House. If it is so, he has lost that individual confidence which every member of the administration should have from his colleagues in this House. For these reasons I have thought it was only right that I should call the attention of the House and the country to a matter which is of serious import in the consequences it may have later on.

As my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) has spoken of this' matter apparently in earnest, I think I owe him the courtesy of an answer,-though I may be permitted to say, at the outset, that I do not think there is much in the contention he has advanced to the committee or the criticism he has made of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson). It is quite true the government is divided into several departments at the head of each of which is Mr. CASGRAIN.
one member answerable for that department to his colleagues, primarily because his colleagues and himself are answerable to parliament. This applies chiefly to the administration of the departments, but it cannot apply in the same way to legislation. No member of the cabinet at the head of the department can take upon himself to introduce legislation unless he has had the view's of the whole cabinet upou it.
In matters of administration, of course he does many things on his own responsibility, of which his colleagues have no knowdedge, but for which they must take responsibility. Upon these the minister is entitled to the glory or the blame of his own acts. That is the sense of the authority which the hon. gentleman has quoted. In matters of legislation, whenever a Bill has to be introduced by a member of the government, whether it be of a purely administrative matter or otherwise, these matters are always debated in council before they are brought to parliament. In such a case I would like to know if when the Bill is introduced it is not altogether within the province of the government to determine what minister is -to take charge of the measure before parliament ? I would call attention to the fact that there is a difference between the English and Canadian systems in our method of administering the affairs of the country. An English minister has much more power of administration and of committing the government than a Canadian minister has. In England meetings' of the cabinet are of rare occurrence ; mouths and months may pass without a single meeting of the cabinet and the business of the government is carried on very largely on the responsibility of individual ministers. But under our system in Canada, according to the practice not alone of this government, but of all governments, meetings of the cabinet are frequent and the cabinet is consulted by every one of its members upon matters of pure administration very, very often. It generally occurs that wrhen a Bill is introduced it is introduced by the minister under whose department it should come. This measure should naturally have been introduced last year by the Minister of Railways and Canals. Unfortunately the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) did not agree to the policy of his colleagues ; he withdrew- suddenly and it fell upon me to take charge of this measure and I did it of course to the best of the ability which I could bring to the question. If my hon. friend (Mr. Blair) had seen upon this question as his colleagues did, if he had agreed to the policy which was accepted by the cabinet, of course he would have introduced this measure. He did not agree and I have just given the reason why I took charge of the measure. This year I again took charge of it ; and why ? The reason is very obvious. Mr. Blair had withdrawn

from the cabinet ; we nad to select a successor and we appointed Mr. Emmerson, the present Minister of Railways and Canals. We appointed him just on the eve of the session. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson), taking charge, just on the eve of the session, of one of the largest and heaviest departments of the government, required a great deal of time and a great deal of labour to prepare for the work of the session, lo prepare his estimates, to carry on the administration of the department, and to carry on the administration of the Intercolonial.
