made a good race for it, and we in New Brunswick were rather glad he had obtained the prize ; but we also hoped that he would give an equivalent to the country for the amount he was receiving. No doubt the right hon. the First Minister gave him advice. The right hon. gentleman was amply able to give him advice. He could have told him very readily: You had better take advice from an older man than yourself. , You had better take advice not only in talking but in acting, and I would suggest that you take advice from the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who at one time said to you don't-don't do it again. That perhaps is the reason the hon. Minister of Railways has not spoken. He has depended so much on the good advice given by the hon. member for South Lanark that he has concluded not to do it again. Whatever may be the reason -whether the government dare not allow the Minister of Railways to speak, or whether he is lacking in courage, it makes no difference which, I claim that it is an insult to *the province which that hon. gentleman is presumed to represent. Now, the hon. gentleman has some powers, and we cannot very well afford to ignore them. He has displayed some of them, too, since he has been in office. He has one power especially. I regret that he is not here, because he would perhaps appreciate it more than any one else in the House. He has the power of vindictiveness. After his recent defeat in St. John, the hon. gentleman showed it very plainly. He did not have to do any talking then to defend the railway. The St. John election had condemned the railway, but there were two good Liberal voters down there neither of whom voted, and the hon. gentleman saw pretty soon that they lost their jobs. There have also been two or three at Moncton since that time. But we need not be very much surprised at these assassinations, for we had it on the word of the right hon. First Minister, who at that time perhaps had not received his knighthood, that no officials would be displaced without due examination, and the opportunity to defend themselves. But there has been no time since then, when these political assassinations have not been taking place. All over the country there has been a cutting off of the heads of gentlemen holding government positions who happened to be independent. We know down in the province of New Brunswick the Minister of Railways was only , carrying out the tactics which he had followed in his own local elections. He kept himself in power by the same means. He had two kinds of ballot papers printed, and he had his minions at the polls, and any government employee who did not cast a certain ballot was dismissed.
It is notorious that since this government came into power, they so conduct provincial politics in the city of Moncton that they have had their' rail-

way employees furnished with ballots and hauled to the polls, and if these employees do not deposit the ballots furnished them, their occupation is gone. And in the city of St. John, Mr. McKeown and his representatives stood at the polls, and woe befell the man who did not present the proper ballot. But, Sir. if the mills of the gods grind slowly, they grind exceeding fine, and they ground Mr. McKeown so fine politically that he will never be heard of as a candidate again. We had hoped to have a defence of this scheme put up by the Minister of Railways himself, and perhaps the right hon. the First Minister will not disdain to accept a suggestion which I make him in all humility. I would suggest that he should go out into the byways and the highways or the corridors or such other places as his hon. colleague may frequent and see if it is not possible to find him and induce him to come to this House and defend this scheme, which so far nas been so poorly defended. Why, take even the defence made by the Minister of Justice, what kind of a defence was it ? He has told us that he is not a railway expert and virtually knows nothing about this proposition from the point of view of a railway man. But he is only in the same boat as the rest of his colleagues. Only a year ago they signed a memo, saying that they knew nothing about the subject, but no doubt they will corral all their followers behind them, when the proper time comes, and these followers will vote straight, and continue to support the government from year to year until the perfume of these wild roses, which are flourishing away out in the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, has been dissipated.

It is rather a strange thing that we are witnessing in this nouse to-day, one the like of which this country has never been treated to in the past and let us hope, will never witness in the future. We are witnessing the pitiful spectacle of a minister of the Crown, either unable or unwilling to give such explanations of the business inaugurated by bis department and proposed to be carried out under his control as this House requires in order that it may pass an intelligent judgment. We have to-day a head of the Department of Railways and Canals-but what kind of a head ?
A deadhead.

A deadhead, says my hon. friend, and the term is not at all inappropriate. But we might also describe him as a titular head, a figure head. According to Webster, a titular head is one existing in letter or in name only, having the title and the honour, but discharging none of the functions of the office. Does not that definition exactly describe the head of the Railway Department to-day-a man who has the name and the honour, but who dis-Mr. GANONG.
charges none of the functions of his office. What is the object in having the government divided into departments ? No doubt the object was to have some responsible head in each department-some one who will be particularly responsible to the House and the country for the conduct of his de-' partment and explain, when required, the work.
What is being done by it. In the Department of Railways and Canals, the particular minister, who is put at the head of that department, should be responsible for every cent of money expended by it, and for the policy which it carries out. And when the policy of the government, which particularly affects that department, is being discussed in the House, that particular minister should be here to explain and defend it. He is supposed to be more conversant with the details than the other members of the cabinet, but what have we in the present instance ? We have a gentleman at the head of the Department of Railways and Canals who is merely its titular head, who knows nothing about his duties, and who does not discharge the functions of his office. He might as well be a merely honorary head. He is not here to explain, he evidently has not familiarized himself with the details of his departmental work, and what information we have obtained regarding the business of that department has been given us, not by the one who. is its responsible head, but by some one whose duties and responsibilities lie particularly in another department. When we have a question to ask in connection with this transcontinental railway scheme-this scheme which comes particularly under the control of the Minister of Railways and the agreement in relation to which has been signed by him-that hon. gentleman is not here to reply. If he were in the upper chamber, we could_ understand somebody being appointed in this House to reply for him. But he is not, he is in this, the popular chamber, yet he is conspicuous by his absence. If this precedent were to be followed, what would become of the business of the country ? We have a Minister of Agriculture to answer questions regarding the Agricultural Department and to explain the policy carried out by his department. We have a Minister of Marine and Fisheries to explain the policy of that department. When anything comes up relating to the Finance Department, we naturally look to the Minister of Finance for information. In matters affecting the customs, we have a Minister of Customs to give us what explanations we require. And so with the Departments of Trade and Commerce and Inland Revenue, the responsible head of each explains' to the House the work and the policy of each. But supposing that in each of these_ departments, the responsible head persisted in remaining silent, and some other minister,

who had nothing to do with his department, had to reply in his place, what result could be expected from such a system. It could only result in confusion worse confounded. Yet when a policy is submitted affecting particularly the Department of Railways and Canals, the carrying out of which must be controlled by the minister of that department, we search in vain for that gentleman. When we have to discuss the details of that policy, that particular man is not to be found. Is not that a travesty on constitutional government ? Is it not treating parliament and the country with contempt ? He is doing that, and that is the only thing. The strength of a government is in proportion to the intelligence, the interest and the businesslike ability with which the members of it manage the details of their several departments. That being so, this minister can certainly bring no strength whatever to the government, because, if he does not manage the details of his department well, we know nothing of it for he gives us no information. .When we ask for information to enable us to judge whether his department is well managed or not, he is not here to answer. What is the explanation of his absence and silence with regard to this most important question ? Is it because of cowardice ? Is it because his colleagues dare not allow him to discharge the functions of his department ? Is it because he is wanting in moral courage to assume responsibilities of his own work before this House ? Is that the explanation ? It may be ; I am not going to say it is. Is it because his colleagues are afraid to trust him, knowing that on this great question he was not in harmony with them a year ago, that he was favourable to government ownership as the policy that should be adopted with respect to railways ? Are they afraid to trust him to-day for fear he might be found not to be in accord with them ? Or is it because he knows nothing of the affairs of his department ? If so, then the government should relieve him from his office and put some one in his place who will master those affairs. Is it that they are afraid that he cannot give the explanations asked for, and that some one else would have to rise in his presence and give them ? Is it because he does not know anything about the aims of this policy when carried out ? Or is it that he will discredit the government in the event of their allowing him to answer the questions ? Which is it V

speechtext: House in Committee on Bill (No. 72) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was endeavouring to find some reasons for the continued absence of the Minister of Railways from this chamber. Several possible explanations occurred to my mind, but on analysing them I have come to the conclusion that they are probably incorrect. The Minister, of Railways cannot be absent because of cowardice, because he usually displays a moderate share of courage. It may or may not be, that the ministry are afraid to trust him to explain their policy, hut upon that subject we have no information. Judging from the remarks of the First Minister this afternoon, it may be that the Minister of Railways knows nothing about the scheme, and that he would discredit the government if permitted to explain it. The premier told us that the Minister of Railways was only recently appointed, and in consequence he had not time to familiarize himself with the work of his department and master the details of this legislation. Well, if this were a matter suddenly sprung upon the House, that explanation would be reasonable, but we must remember that during last session which lasted seven and a half months, this important measure was debated week after week and month after month ; that the government had cabinet council after cabinet council over it, and that they had consulted their supporters in this House and familiarized them with its details so that they might defend it as best they could. In fact, Sir, any member of this parliament with even moderate

ability could not help, but master the details of the measure. Last session the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) was an active participant in the discussion on this Bill in the Eailway Committee and in the House. When a charter was first proposed to enable the Grand Trunk to build from North Bay to Winnipeg, the hon. gentleman opposed it on the ground that such a measure would not meet the needs of the maritime provinces, and he contended that what they wanted was the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Georgian bay, then to use the great water stretches up to the head of Lake Superior, and thence enter that western country. He intimated in the Railway Committee, that Mr. Blair also held that view, and the general assumption was that the member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) was put up to express Mr. Blair's views, because Mr. Blair being then a minister could not record his antagonism to any scheme that might be under the consideration by the government. The member for Westmoreland advocated that principle up to almost the very moment that Mr. Blair resigned, and until there was a portfolio iu sight he never uttered a word in favour of the present Grand Trunk Pacific scheme. Last session in a lengthy and desultory speech that might be dignified by the name of argument, he endeavoured to defend this so-called National Transcontinental Railway, but his whole defence was that the scheme should reach to the maritime provinces, and he did not say a word to condemn the policy which he had advocated over and over again in the Railway Committee. Is he afraid to advocate this scheme now, because of the former convictions which he announced against it in the Railway Committee ? Or, is it that he does not wish to condemn his predecessor in otfice, his political godfather who made him anything he is to-day in public life ? It can hardly be that the Minister of Railways is out of accord with the cabinet, because ministerial responsibility demands that he should be in harmony with his colleagues or else resign. Is it that the Minister of Railways is willing to swallow his convictions, and te sit silent here so long as he can draw the salary and emoluments attached to his office ? I hardly think the hon. gentleman would be guilty of such a thing. Whatever may be the reason, no explanation has been vouchsafed to us by the government. It sometimes happens that when ministers are not in accord with the cabinet, by some strange process of reasoning they bring themselves to the conclusion that the right thing to do is to keep out of the House, we have seen some of the ministers for days and days remain away from this chamber, and in common parlance they are on strike. Is the hon. Minister of Railways Mr. SPROULE.
on strike ? I do. not know, but his conduct looks very much like it.
Whatever it may be, this House should know. Is the hon. gentleman afraid to swallow his convictions 1 If so, he ought to undertsand that when he assumes the responsibility of a portfolio, no matter what his position may have been before, he is bound to defend the measures introduced by the government of which he is a member, whether he is stultifying his previous record or not. So I think that cannot be the explanation. What is the explanation ? No matter how charitable we may be, we must reach some conclusion, and the only conclusion that seems reasonable is that given by the Prime Minister this afternoon-that he does not know anything about the measure. That is the sum and substance of it-that he has not been long enough a minister of the Crown to make himself familiar with the measure which has been before this House for two sessions, and which has been engaging our attention week after week and month after month. He has had at his command all the information available to a minister of the Crown, and he has had subordinates to help him to hunt up information. Surely he should be able to master the details of the measure and to answer questions upon it in this House ; but he has not done so. Therefore I say that we are justified in making this motion as a protest against the government keeping in their employ a minister who is unable to occupy his seat in the House and answer the questions which he should be in a position to answer as the head of an important department, or else resign. We are entitled to make this motion. We do it in order to call the attention of the country to this condition of affairs-to the discreditable spectacle to which we have been subjected for several days, and to which we do not desire to submit any longer. We think it is desirable that it should be exhibited to the country, that the press should take notice of it, that the people should know it, and visit the consequences of it upon the government when the opportunity comes. There is no doubt that the hon. gentleman is a very weak minister, or he would take his place in the House. Why was the Minister of the Interior put up to defend him ? Why is his deputy, the Minister of Justice, put up to argue the case that he should argue ? The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and even the Minister of Agriculture, if my memory serves me, have all spoken on the measure ; and yet the important Minister of Railway and Canals has not had a word to say upon it yet. He is as dumb as an oyster which has gone back into its shell and closed it. It is said that a horse is no better than the most unsound leg he has got and that a ship is no better than

the most rotten plank on it. So a government is no stronger than the weakest minister in it ; and if you judge this government by the Minister of Railways and Canals, I have no doubt that the country has condemned it long ago.

Some days ago, when this Bill was under discussion in committee, my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) raised the question with respect to the construction of the road. I understood him to say that it would be desirable to have the line located and construction proceeded with from a certain point. At that time I said I would have a clause added to the Bill providing for construction from different points, and. in fulfilment of that promise, I have drafted the following clause, which I move to add to the Bill as section 9 :
The work of construction on the eastern division of the Transcontinental Railway shall be commenced as nearly as may be simultaneously at Moncton, at Quebec, - at the point of junction of the eastern division with the branch southerly to a point at or near North Bay or Nipissing junction, and at Winnipeg, and shall be carried on westward from Moncton, eastward and westward from Quebec, eastward and westward from the point of junction aforesaid, and eastward from Winnipeg in such a manner that the section between Winnipeg and Quebec and that between Quebec and Moncton shall he completed, as nearly as practicable, at the same time.
I would like to ask the Minister of Justice if that means that contracts will be called for for the several divisions immediately ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The commissioners will control the giving of contracts, subject, of course, to the approval of the government. But I apprehend that there will be no

question of letting contracts until such time as proper survey and exploration has been made of the route and location of the lines. This, I take it, is simply a direction to the commissioners as to the intention of parliament with respect to the construction of the road. From this the commissioners will understand that the road shall he constructed between Winnipeg and Moncton in such a wav that the several parts shall be completed, as far as possible, at the same time.

That is the desire of parliament, but will the commissioners have instructions that these surveys shall be completed at the same time also ? They may not go on with the surveys. They may carry on the surveys from Winnipeg westward and give the contracts from Winnipeg westwards, but if the surveys on the eastern portion are not completed construction cannot go on, and we do not know when they may be completed. Is it understood that the surveys are to go on and that they will be completed within a reasonable time ?

I would like to ask the Minister of Justice what he meant by this addition to the Bill. As I understand the argument advanced by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). the surveys for the section between Winnipeg and North Bay junction have so far advanced that practically the surveys of the route, showing grades and curves, and all particulars, have been so far advanced that the hon. gentleman was able to tell us. upon the certificate of his geographer, exactly what that section was going to cost; and yet. from the province line near Lake Abitibi, to Quebec, and from Quebec to Moncton, not (one man has been put on the work of survey. I would like to understand exactly what the minister means when he says that a section of the line which has been already surveyed, not simply surveyed in the past two months, but surveys made years back by the old Canadian Pacific Railway by the Ontario government and completed apparently by the Grand Trunk Railway, within 12 months past : that that section was so far advanced that practically two years work had already been done, is to proceed pari passu with sections of the road on which not one dollar has as yet been expended. Looking at it from a practical point of view I should say that we start with the section from Winnipeg to North Bay at least two years ahead of the other sections and with regard to that, I would like to ask the minister, from a practical point of view, how he is going to proceed by equal steps.

'Grand Trunk Company about which the geographer of the Minister of the Interior was able to get information, on this table, and we would be able to see for ourselves

what the Minister of Justice tells us from information, and to have a record upon this table how far those plans have proceeded to this date. Why, Sir, if the information that we have be correct, these plans and these surveys are so useless up to this day that no railway company would undertake SI .000 of obligation upou the strength of them. It has been charged, I do not mean to say it is true, but it is charged, that the instrumental surveys that have been taken by these engineers of which we have heard so much, were so affected by the nature of the country through which those surveys were made that they were absolutely unreliable ; that the Ontario government engineers when going through that country could not rely upon their instruments owing to magnetic differences caused apparently by the ores that were in the soil. If that be so we have got very little information.
For the purpose of one clause of this agreement the hon. Minister of the Interior assures us that it is all right, that we have the most absolute information. When we come to another point we have no information. When we are discussing one branch of the agreement we are told that we have information from Winnipeg to Lake Abitibi, or to the province line, but when it comes to another branch of the agreement we find from the hon. Minister of Justice that we have information not only from Winnipeg to the province line but apparently we have substantial information from the province line to Quebec and from Quebec to Edmonton. Why is it that we have not had that information laid upon the table ? Does the right hon. leader of the government think that it is right and fair and just to the members of this House, to those sitting behind him as well as to those sitting on this side,- that we should be called upon to decide such a question as this is in the absence of any information that it is within the power of the government to furnish us with ? I think not. If what we have heard from the hon. Minister of Justice be accurate, according to the information that is giVen to him, we ought to have had these surveys laid on the table. Some of us, perhaps, would have taken the trouble to have examined the plans. The right hon. leader of the government laid books upon the table containing mountains of information. I took some days to examine those books. I took some time to examine the epitome of these books prepared by a gentleman employed by the government and I must say that the kind of information I got from that epitome was more like a mole hill than a mountain. I mentioned last year the most specific information as to that country which I discovered in the epitome of the mountains of information and I asked anybody to point out anything more

promising or hopeful than that to which I referred. I recollect that no hon. gentleman on the other side of the House was able to find anything beyond what I had found. If I recollect aright the information that was given to us about the agricultural capabilities of that wonderful section was based upon the authority of a gentleman who had once lived at Sorel, and who had been living in this district for some seventeen years, where he had been in charge of the agricultural department of the company by which he was employed. This gentleman had given information as to the agricultural capabilities of the district and he was quite sanguine that the country was capable of producing vegetable products of various kinds. He knew that it would produce vegetables and he had no doubt at all that it would be able to produce wheat. This gentleman, you ascertain when you read on, had been in charge of the tremendous agricultural district of seven acres of land. I went through a good deal of the book and outside of that seven acres I was not able to obtain any information of the many millions of acres through which this railway runs. I then asked some hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who was a better mountaineer than I was and who was capable of going through this mountain of information to say that there was more than I had pointed out, but, I never heard hon. gentlemen opposite say one word on the subject. That is the kind of information we are getting all the time from the government about this project. We ask for information at one stage about the division from Winnipeg to Lake Abitibi and the hon. Minister of the Interior gets up and says that he has it all. He admits that it was very negligent on the part of the railway department not to have it, but he, feeling that that branch of the government was being .sadly neglected takes it upon himself to send his geographer down to Montreal. He does not even ask the Railway Department to give him an experienced railway engineer to go down and look at these plans but he sends a gentleman down who is employed in drawing maps. This gentleman goes down to Montreal. He does not tell us that he saw any of the plans, he does, not tell us that he saw a note of one of the purveys, but he says that he had a conversation with this gentleman, Mr. Stephens, imported from the United States who tells him that it is most satisfactory. He says that up to White Earth Lake he has a location survey. that upon another section he has a preliminary survey, and that upon another section he has no survey but he has no doubt as to what the survey will disclose, and the hon. Minister of the Interior, varnishing that in his usual happy manner, tells us that he has a survey of the whole route to the province line. But, he does not
pretend that he has anything beyond the province line. The hon. Minister of Justice tells us that we have a great deal more, that we have a survey to Quebec, but when we read between the lines of the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice, we find that we have only a survey, apparently, of the St. Maurice River valley and these surveys, I fancy, were not made with the view to the building of this railway at all. These are surveys that have been made in connection with some of these colonization projects of the province of Quebec from the city of Quebec northward up into the Lake St. John district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The St. Maurice district.
' Mr. BARKER. Well, I am very much afraid that no business man will take such surveys, made for such a purpose, as a basis upon which to judge what will be the route, or what will be the cost of this great National Transcontinental Railway. There is just as much difference between the two as it is possible to imagine. There is as great a difference as there is between the old fashioned corduroy road and one of the later style of roads that we have in this country to-day. There is no comparison between a mere colonization railway for the purpose of opening up a back settlement and this magnificent highway, this Transcontinental Railway that we are to have with four-tenths of one per cent gradients and no more than three degree curves, all of the very highest class, which is going to take sixty to eighty cars on every train and which is going to haul them at a dollar per mile according to the experts on the other side of the House. Why, it is absolute absurdity to depend on such statements as those in dealing with the question before the House. But, the hon. gentleman speaks of Edmundston. What about the crossing to Moncton ? I recollect some time ago having a conversation with Sir Sandford Fleming who had surveyed that district across New Brunswick to the Tobique mountains and Sir Sandford Fleming said that it was absolutely impossible, within reasonable limits of cost, to obtain gradients over these mountains that would enable through traffic to be carried at a cheap rate. The hon. gentleman with a push and an enterprise that may be national and that may be characteristic proposes to bind the country to do that, work before he knows that it can be done. It may turn out to be an absolute impossibility but yet the hon. gentleman is going to put it in an Aet of parliament that it shall be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As far as practicable.

Oh, as far as practicable ; the Minister of Justice knows that almost anything is practicable, if you put lots of

money into it, but we are speaking now of a business proposition. We are using words we expect to stand by, and if this government undertakes to construct tbe section in the east without regard to common sense or reason as to the practicability of it, what is the common sense of binding us to go on with this section from Winnipeg to North Bay 7 It ail hangs together ; a chain is no stronger than its weakest link, and if you And in any part of this 1,900 miles of this eastern division that you cannot get the grades that are essential, you knock to pieces the whole structure. And yet the hon. gentleman would propose to bind this whole country to go on as far as practicable, and in the meantime a contract is to be entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific that we are going to do it. They will be encouraged to spend millions of money with our guarantee on the western division, relying on outdoing what is practicable in the east. Does not the minister know that a thing may be practicable, but at an unreasonable and enormous cost; and the Grand Trunk can turn around by and by on us and say ; You have got back after all to our original proposition ; you cannot do this work that you propose for the purpose you intend; we. have our line completed over the mountain and prairie sections, and you have got what we know is practicable, namely, the Winnipeg and North Bay section, and you will have to stay there, and you will compensate us for not giving us that wonderful thing in the east which the right hon. gentleman told us was a ' mine of gold ' to us. Before this House is asked to pass such an amendment as this the hon. gentleman is bound to give us some reasonable information to the effect that what he proposes to do can be done within reasonable limits.

I quite agree with the motion moved by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice; but I have got an amendment here which is a little sharper on the edge than is his. However, if the hon. minister will make a trade with me, I will make a trade with him ; if he will accept my amendment 1 will accept his, and I am sure I will lose nothing in the bargain. I propose :
That the proposed section 9 moved as an amendment to the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following at the end thereof :-
And the said railway after crossing the St. Lawrence river and the Quebec bridge shall run in a southeasterly direction through the counties of Levis and Dorchester, following the course of the Etchemin river up towards Etche-min lake, thence easterly through the province of Quebec to the city of Moncton.
My object in moving this amendment is to show to the government and to the House the necessity for running this railroad along the route that I have been praying the government to adopt. In order to prove to the government the utility of this amendment, let me explain the conditions in the county of Mr. BARKER.
Dorchester, the county of Beauce and all the counties east of Dorchester, lying between the St. Lawrence river and the state of Maine. The area of the county of Dorchester is 602,000 acres, and it comprises seventeen parishes, only two of which are served by a railroad. These two parishes have an area of 35,000 acres, so that 570,000 acres in the county of Dorchester are without railway accommodation. The same remark would apply to the counties of Beauce, Bellechasse, Montmagny, L'lslet and Ka-mouraska. There are probably 3,000,000 acres of land in these counties that are without railway communication, and yet they have been settled for over one hundred years. You can go to the flourishing village of St. George, in the county of Beauce, and in the graveyard you will see there oil the tombstone a statement to the effect that such a man died in 1796 at the age of 89 years ; and at Frampton, in the county of Dorchester, you will see the same thing, showing that these parishes have been settled for over one hundred years, but still they are without railways. The same thing applies to the counties of Bellechasse and Montmagny.
Why-do I say so ? It is because my ancestors settled there in 1636, and several generations of the Morin family have been born and died in that country. By that you can see that the people there have been in what you might call in a quandry for many years, waiting for help from the government, i remember that on the 15th of September, 1895, the right hon. leader of the government-he was then Mr. Laurier, the leader of the opposition-was in the parish of St. Anselm, and he said that if he got into power, his government would be a government of reform and of example. I find no fault with that; but we are waiting for the example, we have been waiting for the railway, and now we are waiting for the reform. My right hon. friend must not be like some of his colleagues, who, if we put a question to them, always reply, the Conservatives did it before. That is no answer at all. My right hon. friend must not say, the Conservatives never gave you a railway. If the Conservatives misbehaved, that is no reason why he should do the same ; because the Conservatives have been voted out of power for their bad doings, and if my right hon. friend does as they have done, he may be voted out of power too. That is reasonable, is it not ? Now, here is another reason why I am asking for the railroad, and you will see what common sense there is in it. Some time ago I put a question on the paper to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. I asked him how much the Quebec Central Railway Company paid to the government for the use of the Intercolonial Railway from Harlaka Junction to Levis, a distance of five miles. I got no answer. I do not know whether the hon. minister was on strike or not. However,

hon. gentlemen know very well that the Quebec Central Railway Company pays something to the government for the use of that road. I have often heard employees of the Quebec Central Railway say that this year the company paid to the government $10,000 ; sometimes they will say $12,000, and sometimes $15,000. I do not know how much it does pay. If you look at the Auditor General's Report you will see that it paid to the government last year $71,925 ; but the book does not explain what this payment was for. I want, as far as I can, to find that out. so as to give the government the point I want to make ; but as I am unable to state what it is, I will give you an idea of it. The route which I have proposed to the, government is this. Start at the Quebec bridge, pass through the parishes of St. Chrysostom and St. Lambert, in the county of Levis, the parishes of St. Isidore, St. Henedine, St. Claire, Ste. Marguerite, St. Malichi, Hampton, and Standon in the county of Dorchester to lake Etehenfln; then follow the Etchemin river through the Alleghany mountains to the south side of the mountains in the county of Bellechasse ; there you strike the Black river that empties into the St. John river ; and continue on the south side of the Alleghany to Lake Pohen-agamook in the county of Kamouraska. That is the route I proposed to the leader of the government last year. Now, the Quebec Central Railway Company got a subsidy last year to aid it to build a railway from a station called Scott in the county of Dorchester to the Quebec bridge, a distance of twenty-two miles. If you build a road by the route I suggest, that company will only have to build four miles of the road, because if the government allow them, they can use this new road which is now before the House. If the Quebec Central Railway Company pay the government $10,000 a year for the use of less than five miles of the road, how much will they pay if they use eighteen miles ? There is a problem that can be solved at any time. The distance from St. George in the county of Beauce to Lake Pohenagamook is 11S miles, according to the map. If the government adopt the route I am now proposing, they will build about eighteen miles of that road. Then, the Quebec Central Railway Company is the owner of both the Quebec Central Railway and the Temiscouata Railway, and they have been trying to build a road on the south side of the Alleghanies. That company is not very wealthy, but it would like to have a connection on the south side of the mountains. If the government build the road I am now asking for, -the Quebec Central will build a branch from St. George to connect with this new road, about twenty or twenty-two miles in length. They could still use the proposed railroad, and they would pay the government in proportion-I do not know how much, but time will tell.
Now, I have brought a good map. If the leader of the government would like to see
it, I will show it to him. Some one says the route that I am laying down is too roundabout. I will admit that it is roundabout. but all the eastern, provinces have contributed to build a railway to the west in order to colonize Manitoba. They built that railway and now they are asked again to help to build another road especially for the people of the west. I believe in being good but not in being too good. It is time that the government should give some help to the people of the eastern provinces as well as to the west. If the government will build the road where I am asking them to build it, they will serve these counties I have mentioned as well as the west. Some people may say that the location I recommend is roundabout. Well, your road will start at Port Simpson and go south-east to Winnipeg and then from Winnipeg to Lake Nepigon. If you will draw a line from Port Simpson to Lake Nepigon, you will find that it will run 175 miles north of Winnipeg, and then from Winnipeg to Lake Nepigon you go a roundabout of forty miles. If you can go forty miles roundabout in the west, why should you not build a road through the county of Dorchester some ten or twelve miles of a roundabout ? Last year the government granted the Quebec Central a subsidy to build 22 miles of road from the Quebec bridge to this place called Scott, and they also granted a subsidy to build a road from St. Francois to St. George in the county of Beauce, a distance of ten miles. I would be very well pleased if the government would insist on the Quebec Central building that ten miles from St. Frangois to St. George. That is very much needed, because the town of St. George is a very flourishing center. It has, however, no encouragement and has been without railways for the last 200 years. The country is a great timber region, with splendid water power and good streams to float the logs down to the St. Lawrence. If a railway were built to St. George, the logs could be collected in a boom there and a mill would be built there to saw them. I do not know whether the government has any power to compel the Quebec Central to build this ten miles of road, but I should be glad if they would use every influence they have to cause that road to be constructed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have to congratulate my hon. friend on his conversion. It may appear somewhat of a death-bed conversion, and possibly my hon. friend may not receive that reward which went to the labourer who came in at the eleventh hour. However, it is satisfactory to know that he is converted and realizes the importance of railway construction through that part of the country. I quite appreciate the value of my hon. friend's information. It goes to corroborate the statements made by those interested in the Bill when it was originally introduced, and shows how necessary it is,

from the standpoint of a practical man such as my hon. friend is, for the development of these counties, that this road should be constructed gt the earliest possible moment Of course, after this road leaves Quebec and. crosses the Quebec bridge to the south side, it must of necessity go through the counties of Levis and Dorchester, then to the county of Bellechasse, and on through the other counties down to Ed-mundston and thence to Moncton. But it is impossible to expect that without accurate location surveys, the government can decide on the route to be selected. All I have to say is that it is intended now, as it was at the very inception of the project by the government to build the road in such a way that all the counties mentioned in my hon. friend's amendment will be beneficially affected.

If the government is going to build a road to satisfy this man or that, the Lord only knows where it ever will be built. What I ask is that before accepting any route, even mine, a survey should be taken and the best location chosen. If the location I advocate is the best, let the government adopt it. But if not, let the government refuse it. That is fair enough. So far I do not see any opposition to the location I suggest. We have here the members from the lower counties. We have the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) who always has his gab open. Here is the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. La-vergne), the hon. member for L'lslet (Mr. Carbonneau), the hon. member for Kamou-raska (Mr. Lapointe)-if they object to the route I propose, let them say so. So far not one has said anything except the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) and he is always open for a bad job.

I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is quite fair in stating that the confession of my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) is a death-bed repentance, because I can vouch for it that since the project of the transcontinental line wras mooted in this House, the hon. member for Dorchester has endeavoured, in every possible way, to ob-'tain from the Minister of Justice a sincere confession that this railway was going to pass through the county of Dorchester, but without having succeeded. Speaking of my hon. friend's motion, as well as the suggestion conveyed in the amendment made by my hon. friend from Dorchester, I would say the feeling expressed by my hon. friend from Dorchester is the feeling entertained by most of the people who take a warm interest in the province of Quebec, and in the time of construction as well as the location of this very important line through that very important province. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has made an attempt this evening, undoubtedly, to give an Mr. FITZPATRICK.
answer to reassure those who entertain this widespread feeling to w'hich I have given utterance more than once in this chamber. But my hon. friend does not go far enough.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The hon. Solicitor General says ' Hear hear,' but we would say ' Hear, hear,' with a great deal more pleasure if there was something more positive, something of a more perfect character in the suggestion of motion of the Minister of Justice. We have an absolute date as to the construction of the western end of the line. We have made a contract there with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we have discussed at great length the question of the date for the completion of the western division. But when we come to that part of the railway that interests the province of Quebec my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, knowing that there is a feeling there that our hopes may not be realized for a great many years, has put in an amendment tending to say that, in the opinion of this House the government part of the line should be begun as soon as practicable and at certain points. I intend to test the feeling of this House upon this question, whether, in justice and fairness to the province while the Grand Trunk Pacific is building its end of the line, we should not have our end of the line built simultaneously, so that the object endeavoured to be realized by this Bill shall be realized from one end of the country to the other at the same time. And I intend asking the House to state its opinion, when this Bill comes up for the third reading that, as the line will be finished throughout the western plains-where everybody claims it should be finished as soon as possible-it should also be finished as far as Quebec at any rate on the eastern division ; and I hope, to be able, when arguing that point before the House, to prove that we have a just claim to the completion as far as Quebec at the same time that its construction is completed in the mountain section. As to the location, knowing my hon. friend from Dorchester, as I do, and being aware of the special information he possesses, I am sure there is no man from the district of Quebec who is so well acquainted with that part of the route which passes south of the St. Lawrence as he is himself. He has studied the question fully and has spent a year at the work, and that part of the country, so little known to most of us, unfortunately not enough known to members of this House, he knows absolutely well. He comes before the committee with a proposition, backed by the knowledge he possesses of that part of the country, that the line should go eastward to his own county, follow the course of the Etchemin river to Etchemin lake and thence eastward. My hon. friend from Dorchester has more than once endeavoured to draw not

only the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) but the Minister of Justice on that point, and I think it is perfectly right and perfectly fair that, before voting upon this important point he should get a declaration, a certain and categorical declaration, from the members of the government whether or not that line is to pass along that direction at any rate without indicating the precise point, where he desires it to pass not only in the interest of the country but in the interest of his own constituency. For my own part, I think that, before this matter is finally disposed of, we should have a declaration from the government, and I intend to invite one as to the course, approximately, that this line is to follow from its entrance into the province of Quebec. We have had it stated on one hand that it is to pass beyond the height of land, beyond the civilized portion of Quebec, and in a direction where, for many years to come, it will not be of any use to the present population of the province. I believe we are entitled to know whether that is the policy adopted by this government, or whether the government will not, more wisely in my opinion-at least that is what I intend to submit to the House-have the line pass in a more southerly direction and located in that part of the province as to which we have absolute and certain knowledge, and where it can be-perhaps not to the extent which a transcontinental line might have been if carried out on other lines-of great value to the province of Quebec. I sympathize with the proposition of the hon. member for Dorchester. I think he has good reason for it, and I intend to vote for it. And I may say that, although I am glad to hear the Minister of Justice admit the principle that we are entitled to state now upon this most important measure that there must be simultaneous construction upon the line at certain points. But his motion is not categorical enough, it does not specify the time with sufficient clearness. I intend voting against it, reserving my right on the third reading to make a motion that will make it certain that the work will be carried out according to the intent of the Prime Minister when he announced the Bill, that it is to be from the outset and throughout its execution a transcontinental railroad from wrhich every portion of the country will profit at the same time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend has further convinced me that as the end approaches more light is breaking in upon the hon. gentlemen opposite from the province of Quebec. If my hon. friend is in sympathy, as he apparently is with the object the government had in view of constructing this Transcontinental Railway so that it may benefit Quebec and the maritime provinces.
I think he might usefully employ his time in converting his friends and associates on that
side of the House. The hon. gentleman is not forgetting the statement made by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) who prayed heaven that this road east of North Bay would never be built. My hon. friend does not forget that to-night the argument of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) was altogether in opposition to the construction of the line or any necessity for the construction of the line east of North Bay. I can quite understand that my hon. friend from Dorchester has a large amount of information with respect to the country east of Quebec and between Quebec and Edmundston. And it is because of the information he possesses that his opinion is so valuable. He is urgent, he is insistent, that this road should be built. We agree with him up to that point, we know he is correct, we know that his information is accurate, we know that he speaks from his own personal knowledge, and that the information he has is the result of an investigation which he made, prompted, no doubt, by the suggestion of the government last session that this road would be built. Now, the only point of difference between the hon. member for Dorchester and myself is this-he insists on a specific location of the line after it crosses the River St. Lawrence going eastward.
Undoubtedly, to any one who knows anything of the geography of the country between (Edmundston and Quebec, this line must of necessity go through Levis, and through Dorchester, and through Bellechasse, and through Montmagny, and through L'lslet, and through Kamouraska. It cannot get to Edmundston otherwise, owing to the geographical conditions. But as to the precise location within these general lines, it is impossible for the government, however great their confidence in the opinion of the hon. member for Dorchester may be, to accept his location. We have to trust to the engineers for that. We know very well that when the time comes to locate the line definitely we will have the advantage of the views of the hon. member for Dorchester, and we know him to be patriotic enough to put that information at the disposal of the engineers, and to do all he can to enable the engineers to locate the line. It may be-and I speak from my personal knowledge, for, as the hon. member for Dorchester knows, I have some acquaintance with the geography of that district-that my opinion would concur with his respecting the location ; I think the location which he pointed out is an admirable location, but I would not attempt to set my opinion up when it is a question of engineering. This is a matter for the engineers to finally determine,, and that is all we can say. So far as the construction of the eastern section is concerned, it is the desire of the government to proceed as rapidly as possible. Not only is it their desire, but their fixed determination, to have that road ready as soon as the

33 70
road west to tlie Rocky Mountains is built. That is our fixed determination, and we will have that road built in such a way that it may be of the greatest good from a national standpoint; not that it may be a benefit from any sectional standpoint, but in such a way as to be a benefit to the whole country from Winnipeg to Moncton. What we wish is to consider the road as one unit, from the standpoint of the general interests of Canada, and X trust I am sincere in the wish that whatever government may be in power once the country is committed to this project that road will be constructed in its entirety, notwithstanding some hasty expressions of opinion from the other side to the effect that if the opposition came in this whole scheme would be cancelled. I hope the scheme will be carried out in its entirety, from the standpoint of the country at large and to the general interests of the whole community.

I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is quite fair, whenever an effort is made on this side of the House to make this measure as perfect as it can possibly be made, to repeat that light is coming to this side of the House, that we are all gradually becoming converted to this scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And we welcome the converts.

It is a joke that may pass muster once or twice, but it becomes stale after a while. For my own part, I have listened very patiently to very long speeches in this House upon this important subject, and I feel that I am obliged to say I have not changed my idea at all from the beginning, but I take it that it is going to beoome law. I meet people every day who ask me if there is any chance of this Bill passing this House, and I always say there is a very great chance. Taking that view, I desire to see it as perfect as possible. 1 do not think the Minister of Justice is quite fair to the member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin). The member for Dorchester knows that this transcontinental line may pass through a corner of his constituency, but he has given study to the subject, and as early as last year he developed, not only before this House, but to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice individually, the theory which he has developed this evening, that the railway, to be a good railway, should be located as he has stated, not across the corner of his constituency, but down through the heart of it, along the Etchemin river. The minister has had time since last year to make up his mind as to whether the plan advocated by the hon. member for Dorchester is a good one. ' As regards the location and the time of construction, my hon. friend last year knows there was a great difference between the situation between the western and the eastern divisions. The Grand Trunk has been limited to a certain number of years, Mr. FITZPATRICK.
but we cannot get any limitation in regard to the line passing through the older provinces. We have simply been told that it was the intention of the government to build the eastern section, and this evening the only assurance we have from the Minister of Justice is that as far as practicable the eastern division will be begun simultaneously with the western division. Surely we are entitled to have some precise date fixed by the government, and are justified in asking the government to tell us, on the third reading of this Bill, whether the section from Winnipeg to the west will be built throughout at the same time as the section from Winnipeg to Quebec. I, for one, believe, as I believed when I spoke on the second reading of this Bill, that it would have been better in the province of Quebec to spend the same amount of money in another way upon railway construction, but I take it whatever we thought of that subject has been brushed aside. We are going to have this railway built upon the general principles laid down when the Bill was introduced last year, and under those circumstances I say that we in Quebec are entitled to a categorical declaration from the govern ment embodied in this Bill that it will be located according to certain lines in Quebec, that it will pass in a certain known direction, and that it will be built within a certain specified time.
