Amendment (Mr. Fitzpatrick) agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have another amendment to propose. I beg leave to propose :
That the following clause be added at the end of the Bill entitled an Act to amend the National Taranscontinental Railway Act. Section 9 of the National Transcontinental Railway Act is hereby amended by striking out the word * three ' in the fourth line thereof and substituting the word ' fourth.'
The intention is to provide for four commissioners as was suggested by the right hon. Prime Minister last night and for the reason explained by him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the amendment passes I would like to say that I do not regard it as necessary or wise. I do not regard it is necessary because I think three commissioners can do this work quite as effectually and quite as thoroughly as four can. I do not regard it as wise, because, if an even number is appointed, there may be possibly an equal division of opinion, two on one side and two on the other. I am under the impression that the change has been influenced not so much by the public interest as by the political necessity of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.

Mr. Chairman, I see in one of the papers that the appointment of

this additional commissioner has been made for the purpose of making a position for the hon. premier of the province of Quebec. I see his name mentioned and 1 see it stated that the government had to settle with him. I understood when discussing this matter some time ago that the government had decided to take over the charter that the premier of Quebec holds for a road from Quebec to Winnipeg. I thought they had settled with him in that way without giving him this position as one of the commissioners.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What charter does the hon. gentleman refer to ?
Mr. .1. D. REID. Is there not a charter for a road between. Quebec and Winnipeg- for the Trans-Canada Railway ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He has no interest at all in that.
every hon. gentleman knows that every minister who held a portfolio was able to defend his portfolio and defend any Bill for which he was responsible.
You did not think so at the time.
The hon. gentleman knows that it was not necessary to ask a minister to do that, that , he did it upon his own responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope that the discussion which took place in the afternoon on the motion that the chairman leave the chair will not be revived because we have disposed of it. The question now is on the amendment before the committee.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is all in the hands of your friends.
I understand that the premier of Quebec controls that charter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not to the extent of a farthing.

I am speaking to it. I was explaining the position of the ministers and the change that has taken place to-day as compared with their course when they first assumed power. We have a government bringing forward this Bill and there are only three ministers running the government-the right hon. leader of the government, the bon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Justice. These are the only ministers who are competent

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope that the hon. gentleman will not require to be reminded again that the question under discussion is the propriety of changing ' three ' to ' four.'

Well, I am trying to get some information in connection with this matter. I would like to know if I am not in order in asking why it is that the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals is not present. We have not been able to get any information whatever on the amendment which the government have moved. The right hon. Prime Minister, the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Minister of Finance are the only ministers who have been taking part in this debate. Am I not in order in asking for information from other ministers, who are responsible for this Bill ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, the hon. gentleman is perfectly justified in asking for information, but if they do not wish to give the information the hon. gentleman has no right to go on and discuss a question not under consideration at the present time.

BORDEN, i think my hon. friend the member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) is perfectly in order in calling attention to the fact that a minister of the Crown charged with the Department of Railways and Canals is not here to give the information which he should be expected to give There is no doubt of that. He is absolutely in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot see it in that light at all. We had a discussion this afternoon when the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) ashed an lion, gentleman to move a special motion for the purpose of getting it in and if the hon. gentleman is now in order in speaking upon that motion again I do not understand what the rules of the House are.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend is absolutely in order in asking for information from the hou. Minister of Railways and Canals upon a question as to whether three commissioners are not more in the public interest than four commissioners and in calling attention to the fact that the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals is not here for the purpose of giving information upon that and other subjects in connection with this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Certainly, he is perfectly at liberty to go that far.

That is the very point which I am making, but if the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals is not present, if the right hon. leader of the government sends him out of the House-the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was here a few moments ago and he has now disappeared-we cannot get the information from him. If the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Finance, or the Minister of Justice, cannot give us the information-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the information ?
I want to know why you are appointing four commissioners instead of three. An amendment to that effect has been moved without a single word of explanation from the First Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been upbraiding some ministers with not being present in the House, but if he himself had set the good example of being in the House yesterday, he would have heard the explanation which I gave last night.
I may not have been in the House at the moment
Oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman said that the whole matter would be discussed on the Bill, and that is what my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) is doing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He wants information which I gave last night, and if he wishes me to repeat it now, I shall be happy to do so.
Well, I would like to hear it again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I stated last night that if four commissioners were ap-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
pointed there would be one for Ontario, one for Quebec, one for the maritime provinces and one for the west.

The right hon. gentleman selected three commissioners in the first instance, but he has not told us it he had discovered any further work for them to do which requires a fourth commissioner. It is due to the opposition, the House and to the country, that the Minister of Railways should be here to answer these questions. We do not know whether he approves of this amendment or not. ,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr, Ingram) is not so ignorant as he wants us to believe. He knows very well the opinion of the Minister of Railways on this subject; he knows that if the opinion of the government was not the opinion of the Minister of Railways, he would resign.
It is currently reported throughout the country that not only the Minister of Railways, but several other ministers are not in accord with this scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Don't believe it.

And as a proof of that report we have the fact that the Minister of Railways will not appear in the House. It is also reported that these ministers will either have to vote for this measure or resign their positions, and that they are swallowing their principles to remain in the cabinet. The only thing we know from the Minister of Railways is what he stated in the Railway Committee last year, and his statement then was in opposition to this measure. Why does not the Prime Minister let the Minister of Railways and Canals come into the House ? I am very glad that the Minister of Railways has at last appeared, and I want to know from him why a fourth commissioner has been appointed at additional expense to the country when three commissioners are sufficient ?
What particular section of the country would the hon. gentleman deprive of representation ?

I would choose three of the best men in the Dominion irrespective of what province they might come from. Dwould not use the job for political purposes, the same as the government did when they appointed the Railway Commissioners.

The Prime Minister has given no sufficient reason why a fourth [DOT]commissioner should be appointed. He has not answered the proposition, that suppose there should be an even division of opinion amongst the four commissioners ; two being ranged on one side and two on the other, how would the difficulty be met ? If the

result is going to be like the Alaska Boundary Commission, then we want none of it. We are found fault with because we want information from the Minister of Railways, and the right hon. gentleman told me that I had the right to assume that the Minister of Railways agreed with the cabinet on this proposition. I point out to the Prime Minister that the records of the House prove that I have no right to assume any such thing, because I can quote from the statement made by the Minister of Railways last year, language in direct opposition to the amendments moved by the Minister of Justice. In the debates that occurred in this House last year, the Minister of Railways and Canals used this language :
You may put in this charter, or add to it a clause which you may think would guarantee to the people of Canada an all-rail route over Canadian soil, and guarantee that the exports shall go through Canadian ports, but you wil cot accomplish what you purpose to do.
The amendments moved by the Minister of Justice to this Bill are not in accordance with that statement ; and I ask the Minister of Railways and Canals if he will get up to-night and say that he entertains the same view now that he entertained last year on this question. If he will not, I have a right to assume that he is not in accord with the amendment moved by the Minister of Justice to-night. What other conclusion can we arrive at ? If the right hon. leader of the government has ordered the Minister of*Railways and Canals not to say a word on this question, then I would like to know if that is the position the cabinet has taken. I ask the Minister of Railways and Canals to tell what is the additional labour to be performed by this fourth commissioner. The hon. gentleman is at the head of the department; will he give us an answer ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Question, question.

The government are certainly in a very peculiar position. I am going to put it as the ordinary elector puts it. The people of this country are paying a large salary to a cabinet minister who fills one of the most important positions in the government, and who will r.ot rise in his place to answer a question on -a matter involving an expenditure of thousands of dollars. I ask the right hon. leader of the government what he would have done previous to 1896, when occupying the position of leader of the opposition, if the Conservative government of that day had had a minister in the same position as the hon. Minister of Railways. In 1894 or 1895, when a certain hon. gentleman be longing to what was called the colony, spoke o" some of the cabinet ministers of that day as being green grocers, and not 1071
fit to fill their positions as cabinet ministers, what did the hon. gentlemen opposite say ? They upheld that hon. gentleman in making that charge. Yet I am in a position to state that no Conservative minister ever refused to the opposition an answer to any civil question they asked in this House during the time I have been a member. Let us be as courteous as we please, are wo to be told that a minister occupying the important position of Minister of Railways, is going to refuse to answer a civil question which the members of the opposition have a right to ask ? Is that the position the government are going to take when they go to the people, and when tlie right hon. gentleman is asked, as he will be asked, whether he had a minister in his cabinet who refused to answer a civil question.
It was answered fifty times.

The hon. gentleman from West York (Mr. Campbell) would fill the position better. The hon. gentleman talks while he is sitting, but the Minister of Railways will not speak either sitting or standing. I ask the hon. gentleman if he xv ill give us an answer ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I gave my hon. friend an answer a moment ago, and he said that the answer was not good and sufficient. That is his judgment. In my judgment it is good and sufficient. It is the answer of the government, in which all members of the government are unanimous. That is all I can say. In my judgment it is a good answer ; in my hon. friend's judgment it is not. How-are w6 to decide ? It wil! be for the people to judge between us, whether it is a good answer or a bad answer.

The right bon. gentleman will admit that we are quite within our right in asking w-hat the duties of that commission are to be. The right hon. gentleman has not stated, unless it be to^get Ontario, and Quebec, the Maritime and Noi'thwest provinces each a representative on that commission.

In the course of the remarks of the hon. gentleman representing Grenville (Mr. Reid), he said that he w-anted to get information ; but he took a very peculiar course in seeking for information, w-hen he stated that the Prime Minister of the province of Quebec was the owner o1 the Trans-Canada charter from Quebec to Lake Winnipeg. I happen to know something about the affairs of the Trans-Canada Railway Company, more than any other man in this House, and probably more than any man outside of this House ; and I can make the statement that the Prime Minister of the province of Quebec, Mr. S. N. Parent, never had anything to do with the Trans-Canada Railway Company, and

lias nothing to do with it at this moment.
I can further state that the promoters of the Trans-Canada Railway somewhat resented the attitude of the Prime Minister of the province of Quebec towards that railway in this respect, that up to the last moment, he would not promise any land grant to help them to promote or finance their scheme. This simple fact is clear evidence that he never had anything to do with it. The charter of the Trans-Canada Railway Company is still in the possession of the same people in whose possession it was two years ago.
Does the hon. member know who the president of that road is ?
William Price, lumber merchant, of the city of Quebec.

Getting back to the question before the committee, as to whether the number of commissioners for the construction of the eastern division of the Transcontinental Railway should be three or four, I must say that I have listened very carefully to the answer given by the right hon. leader of the government, but that I am not very deeply impressed with the reason which he has advanced. Not long ago we had an important commission appointed in connection with railway matters under the Railway Act. Three were appointed-one to represent Ontario, one, Quebec and another. New Brunswick, but it was not thought necessary that any commissioner should be appointed for Manitoba or the Northwest. It seems to me that the government should have followed that precedent. However, I do not care whether the number be three or four, if the cost he not increased. I apprehend that the gentlemen appointed commissioners will be paid very handsome salaries for a very considerable number of years-from seven to ten years. If it is the intention of the government not to increase the aggregate cost, of the commission when the number of commissioners is increased from three to four. I would have no objection to the. increase in number, though I think three commissioners quite sufficient, more especially as the greater part of their work will be reviewed by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The addition of one more member to the commission would mean the addition of one more salary.
What is to be the salary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It. is not fixed yet ?

Has the government any idea of what it will be ?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Yes, but I would not like to commit myself.

This is an important point, as the commission will last some eight Mr. TALBOT.
or ten years, and we are entitled to the information.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Certainly.

I think that this commission will involve very considerable cost, but I would be prepared to acquiesce in even another commissioner being appointed, if their tenure of office was independent. They are, however, to be removed at will. They should hold exactly the same position as the Auditor General. At any rate, they should not be removed without cause, which cause should be denounced to parliament as in the case of a lieutenant governor.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, I will take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration and advise parliament at the next stage of the Bill. Last year when a similar question was raised, the government undertook, before the Bill was finally passed, to announce what the salary would be. That course will be pursued on the present occasion. The government will announce on the third reading what the salaries will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

What new light have the government received on this subject this last year which has induced them to appoint four instead of three commissioners ? The only explanation given by the First Minister is that the government desire to have each province represented. That would seem to indicate that they have a greater regard for tlfe distribution of patronage than the fitness of the men, because otherwise there would be no reason why these men should be selected from three or four provinces. I am convinced that the best results would be obtained by selecting men on account of their fitness regardless of where they live.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I stated yesterday that one of the important duties of the commissioners would be to have surveys made and a route located. All parties are anxious to see the railway built from Winnipeg to Moncton, and in order that every section of the country may be served, we have been advised that every province should be represented on the commission.
Is there any reason to suppose that four commissioners would build the road more rapidly than three Y ,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Doubt has been expressed again and again regarding the extension of the line to Quebec and Moncton, and we want to absolutely assure to every section that the whole road will be built.
Why not make the number ten ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are not ten sections.

If parliament orders the road to be built, we have the assurance of the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister that it will be, and that should, at least in the opinion of the government, be sufficient assurance to the country. I wish to ask another question. There will be some intermediary between this commission and the government. Will they do their business through the Railway Department or direct through council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a point that I have not considered at all-whether they should report direct to the Minister of Railways or to council. I suppose they would report to the Minister of Railways, but I must say frankly to my hon. friend that we have not considered that.

I would like to ask the minister if this commission will sit as a board and will have power to decide locations after having had surveys laid before them V And in ease they were divided equally on any matter, what would the result be-how would the matter be finally decided ?
'Sir WILFRID LAURIER. If they are divided, there will be nothing decided. They will have to make a recommendation to the government. They are not to sit as a board ; they simply advise the government. They cannot give a contract above $10,000 unless the contract is sanctioned by the Governor in Council.

Since they must report to the government in some way, I would suggest that they should report direct to council. The evidences we have of the Minister of Railways having lost his voice, or being unable to deal with this important transaction, must lead us to believe that the commission would be more successful if they did business direct with council and entirely ignored the Department of Railways and Canals.

I was surprised to hear the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) make an announcement that was equivalent to expressing a want of confidence in the commissioners. He told us, if I mistake not, that the object of appointing four commissioners was that there might be no difficulty, and that everything might be carried on fairly for all the sections. Does the right hon. gentleman give the committee to understand that any of these commissioners would perform his duty any less in regard to one section than to another V Surely he is not going to appoint any one who would for a moment think of giving one section advantage over the other. I should imagine you could find men who could be depended upon, and I am unable to see that there is any more security in four commissioners than there would be in three. No section of Canada is more interested in this road than another. British Columbia is interested in
having the western section completed, but it is also interested in having the road built across the prairies and so to the Atlantic coast. The same is true of the Northwest Territories, of Manitoba and the other provinces. Why create a sentimental halo over this whole project ? It seems to me there is no reason in that. Surely, if the right hon. gentleman appoints commissioners," they ought to be capable men, and men above suspicion that they will help one section as against another. If they would consider one section above another, they would be corrupt and utterly unworthy of being entrusted with such important 'duties as these commissioners will be expected to perform. While I listened with interest to the reasons the right hon. gentleman has given, yet those reasons seem very extraordinary. They are a sad reflection upon the three commissioners. His reasons for adding a fourth were a statement, in as plain English as could be well used, that the three commissioners are not to be trusted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The commissioners that we shall appoint. I am glad to say, will be above reproach. More, like Caesar's wife, they will be above suspicion. I cannot be sure, of course, that they will not be suspected by my hon. friend (Mr Clancy), but I am sure there will be more security in four commissioners than in three.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would remind my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that Caesar had only one wife, not four.

The reason given by the Prime Minister for appointing four commissioners is that he desires to assure the different parts of the Dominion that the government intended to carry this railway project through from the maritime provinces to the Pacific coast. Is it necessary to do this in order to assure the people that the road will be built V Surely the Prime Minister must suppose that every province takes it for granted that he means what he says when he asks parliament to put this Bill through. In that case, it should not be necessary to appoint another commissioner in order to give confidence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to isay that, though we have given our best attention to this measure, and though we have shown that we were very much in earnest, still, sitting near my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) there are those who tell us that it will not be built. There are some doubting Thomases on the other side of the House.

The only part there was any doubt about was the part from Quebec to Moncton, and I have been trying all evening to get some information with regard to that part of the road : but I am sorry to say the Minister of Railways is still muzzled and is not able to give us

uriy information. I suppose it is to give assurance as to that part of the road that the extra commissioner is to be appointed, and that he will be from the province of New Brunswick.
I take it that the Prime Minister hopes to establish confidence on his side of the House by appointing this extra commissioner. If that is his object, it seems to me he might as well save the salary.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Bill as amended, reported.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.

speechtext: Shall we proceed with the third reading to-morrow

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
